items.title: OD-RULES-017 left env/doc/docs open: the last 5 self-check abbreviation findings need a scoped-approval or structural exemption
items.why:
OD-RULES-017 (accepted) resolved 25 of the 30 self-check abbreviation findings that quote a term they are about, and explicitly left five open by design, not oversight: crates/languages/nomos-lang-rust/tests/corpus/claims.rs (Has_Misplaced_Inner_Doc, Line_Is_Misplaced_Inner_Doc), crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/tests/governing_records_are_present/supersession.rs (Test_Adr_Doc_001_...), crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/concurrency_text.rs (..._Docs_Own_Unmarked_Example) and crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/script_discipline.rs (..._Accept_Env_Shebang). Its own "What This Record Does Not Do" section names the reason and the shape of what would resolve it: "doc"/"docs"/"env" are common enough English-word abbreviations that a whole-workspace standards.json approval (the channel OD-RULES-017 used for chk/vs/rs/rc/cmp/lf/ms/nth) risks silently masking a real abbreviation elsewhere -- these five sites use the words as Rust's own "doc comment" term of art and the literal POSIX env command, not as shorthand for "document"/"environment", but nomos.cap.words.policy has no way to scope an approval to a site or a file, only the whole workspace.

This is a real gap, not a mechanical follow-up: nomos.cap.words.policy / standards.json would need a scoped-approval shape (e.g. per-file or per-rule-id) that does not exist today, which is capability work, or Check_Abbreviations itself needs a structural exemption in the shape of its existing two (a name nobody chose) rather than a vocabulary addition. Territory intentionally does not commit to either shape.

Whichever is chosen is implemented and the five sites above report clean. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

- script_discipline.rs's ..._Should_Accept_Env_Shebang: the enclosing test group is already Portable_Shebang; "the recommended/portable form" describes the outcome the assertion actually checks without naming the literal env command, which the test body's string literal (#!/usr/bin/env bash) still names precisely.

items.title: Sleep-based-synchronization and retry-until-green rules in a new flakiness_text.rs
items.why: code-standards' check-flaky-tests (shared package rules/general/testing/shared/flakiness, judge.go/site.go) enforces two rule docs, sleep-based-synchronization.md and zero-flake-policy.md, neither yet ported. Read rust_flakiness.go and go_flakiness.go directly: Rust matches a fixed sleep-call vocabulary (thread::sleep, tokio::time::sleep, async_std::task::sleep, spin_sleep::sleep) inside test functions via tree-sitter, plus a fixed retry-attribute vocabulary (retry, flaky_test, flaky, retry_test) immediately preceding a decorated fn; Go matches only time.Sleep inside Test-prefixed functions in _test.go files and explicitly does not implement retry detection for Go (no attribute syntax to settle it on, stated as a deliberate limit in go_flakiness.go's own doc). zero-flake-policy's other prohibition, silent disabling with no reason, is already covered by a different tool's already-ported rules (a-skipped-test-states-why, a-disabled-test-states-why) so only the retry-until-green half is new here. Neither vocabulary is repository-configurable (fixed lists in code-standards itself, no standards.json block), so per OD-RULES-011's own test this is a leaf module, not a nomos.cap.*.policy capability. Text-scanning without the real tools' tree-sitter/go-ast precision: test-scope is approximated the way this crate's other *_text.rs rules already document doing (Is_Test_Or_Example_Source for file-level test/example paths, widened here to also start scanning from a file's first #[cfg(test)] or #[test] marker onward, since most Rust unit tests live inline in an otherwise-production file and file-path-only scoping would miss the exact case check-flaky-tests' own doc measured against a real corpus).
items.done_when: crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/flakiness_text.rs implements Check_Sleep_Is_Not_Synchronization (rule id sleep-based-synchronization; Go+Rust, fixed sleep-call vocabulary, marker escape hatch 'flakiness: allow' same-line, own-file self-exemption) and Check_A_Test_Does_Not_Retry_Until_Green (rule id zero-flake-policy; Rust only, fixed retry-attribute vocabulary immediately preceding a fn, same marker escape hatch) with unit tests covering each judgment, its marker exemption, its test-scope boundary (a sleep in production code is not flagged), and its own-file self-exemption. checks.rs declares mod flakiness_text and re-exports both functions and both rule-id constants; lib.rs's own pub use checks::{...} re-export block carries them too, since that is what makes them reachable from the crate root at all (found mid-implementation: omitting it leaves every function in the new module dead-code-warned, not merely undocumented). The nomos-rules public surface snapshot is reblessed. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

items.title: gate/tests.rs's two real-run tests judge the wrong tree under cargo test, because their root is a bare relative dot
items.why:
Test_Host_Variant_Should_Compose_Into_A_Real_Run_That_Judges_This_Workspaces_Own_Tree and Test_Read_Source_Should_Underlie_A_Real_Runs_RunId_Report (crates/host/nomos-cli/src/gate/tests.rs) both build their GateCommand with root: PathBuf::from("."), a path relative to the test process's own working directory. `cargo test` sets that to the crate's own manifest directory (crates/host/nomos-cli), not the workspace root, so both tests silently walk only that one crate's own tree rather than the workspace `nomos check --root .` and the real gate step (`cargo run ... -- gate run --root .`, invoked from the workspace root) actually judge.

This surfaced now (2026-09-02) because the workspace self-check just reached zero real blocking findings for the first time (OD-RULES-017/018): with nothing genuinely wrong workspace-wide, the gap became visible as a spurious failure -- crates/host/nomos-cli/tests/platform_std_seam.rs has two test names containing "std", which is approved in the real, root-correct standards.json but invisible to nomos.cap.words.policy resolution when root resolves to the crate directory instead (no standards.json exists there, so the capability comes back unavailable and the additions don't apply).

This crate already has the fix in two other files, both unit- and integration-test: crates/host/nomos-cli/tests/check_command.rs's private Repository_Root() (env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") joined with "../../..", an absolute path immune to cwd) and crates/host/nomos-cli/src/agent/tests.rs's own copy of the identical helper. gate/tests.rs has neither and is the one module in this crate still using a bare relative ".".

Both failing tests' own doc comments claim to "exercise the same command CI actually runs" and "must agree with itself end to end" -- a claim that is false as currently written, since CI's `cargo run` (cwd = workspace root, matching a person's own invocation) and this file's `cargo test` (cwd = crate root) resolve "." to different trees. The doc comments are not wrong about intent, only about whether the code delivers it.
items.done_when: gate/tests.rs gains its own Repository_Root() helper, matching check_command.rs's and agent/tests.rs's existing pattern exactly (env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") three parents up). Test_Host_Variant_Should_Compose_Into_A_Real_Run_That_Judges_This_Workspaces_Own_Tree and Test_Read_Source_Should_Underlie_A_Real_Runs_RunId_Report build their GateCommand with that root instead of PathBuf::from("."); every other test in the file that uses "." either tests argument parsing only or scopes to a location that does not exist regardless of root, so it is untouched. cargo test -p nomos-cli --bin nomos is green, including both previously-failing tests, run from both the crate directory and the workspace root (confirming the fix is genuinely cwd-independent, not accidentally still relying on where the test happened to run from).

None is a lazy synchronization substitute the rule exists to catch: wait.rs:68's own real Launcher polls a live child with the identical POLL_INTERVAL-sleep pattern in production code (correctly unflagged, since it carries no #[cfg(test)]/#[test] marker for the rule's file-scope to reach) -- drain.rs/spawn.rs's Awaited() helpers wait on the exact same kind of detached, channel-less, poll-only thread this crate's own module doc (drain.rs's Drain doc comment) explains is deliberate, not an oversight. tests.rs:401 has no event to synchronize on at all -- it is proving an absence (nothing wrote after the kill) over a fixed window, which polling cannot remove, only shrink.

items.title: naming-clarity: vague grab-bag names, a fifth nomos.cap.words.policy dimension
items.why: code-standards' check-naming-clarity (rules/general/style/checks/naming/word-choice/check-naming-clarity, main.go + kernel/config/words/{config.go,defaults.go}) flags a declared name whose first word is on a repository-configurable vague-word list (default 20 words: data, do, helper, helpers, manager, managers, object, objects, process, processor, service, services, stuff, thing, things, util, utils, utility, handler, wrapper), extendable via standards.json's words.vague and subtractable via words.vague_exempt -- the exact same Config shape words.approved_abbreviations already uses, read by the same Vague_Word(name, lists.Vague) -> (word, bool) function abbreviations.rs already mirrors the sibling of (Name_Abbreviations). Structurally this rule is a near-exact twin of the already-ported abbreviations.rs: same symbols/syntax-payload iteration, same trait-impl exemption (a trait fixes a member's name), same use-binding exemption (an import names something declared elsewhere), same struct-field judgment, same Split_Identifier_Words word-splitter. It is repository-configurable (vague/vague_exempt are real standards.json dimensions, not a fixed compiled-in list), so per OD-RULES-011 this extends the existing nomos.cap.words.policy capability (contract, provider, WordsPolicyPayload wire format) rather than creating a new leaf module or a new capability family. items.title: named-fields-over-positional-variant-payloads: a multi-field tuple enum variant
items.why: code-standards' check-tuple-variant (rules/general/style/checks/data-and-values/data-shape/check-tuple-variant, main.go + shared rules/general/style/shared/variantshape/{variant.go,analyzer.go} + language-kernels/programming/rust/rustlang/rust_variant_shape.go) flags a Rust enum variant whose payload is positional (tuple-form) with two or more members: Point(f32, f32) compiles with x and y swapped, so the compiler cannot police the order the way it would a named struct-form variant. Verified against the real Go implementation, not the doc prose: is_Variant_Unambiguous exempts only single-member payloads (Some(T), Ok(T), newtypes) and fires on EVERY payload of two or more members regardless of whether the member types repeat -- has_Repeated_Type only changes the finding's MESSAGE text, never the verdict, which is narrower and more accurate than named-fields-over-positional-variant-payloads.md's own prose ('two or more fields of the SAME TYPE'), a doc-vs-implementation drift this port follows the implementation on, per this crate's established practice. Three code-standards rule-doc ids all cite this one tool for this one judgment (named-fields-over-positional-variant-payloads, multi-field-variants-use-struct-form, and a third at a different doc path, multi-field-enum-variants-use-struct-form, that the second doc explicitly points to as its real authority) -- real upstream doc drift, not three judgments; this port uses one canonical id, the fullest MUST-severity prose actually filed in check-tuple-variant's own doc directory. rust_variant_shape.go's own doc comment records a real corpus lesson worth porting faithfully: a first cut assumed an enum's opening brace sits on the same line as  and silently found zero across a 4,515-file corpus, because the real corpus writes Allman-style braces (enum header on one line,  on the next); the fix tracks whole-file brace depth and only commits an enum open once a  actually arrives, on that line or any later one. This crate has never ported a whole-file brace-depth state machine before (existing *_text.rs rules deliberately avoid it), but the real algorithm here is small and bounded (one depth counter, one pending-header string, ported from a ~60-line Go source read in full) and the same naive per-line strings.Count('{')/('}') the real tool itself uses (also naive about strings/comments mid-line, a stated and accepted limitation, not a gap this port needs to close beyond it). The escape hatch (// tuple-variant: allow <reason>, reason required) IS portable here, unlike naming-clarity's marker in the sibling item: this rule reads raw source text directly and carries its own real line numbers from the scan itself, never routing through nomos_cap_syntax::PayloadItem's line-less payload.
items.done_when: A new crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/enum_shape.rs implements Check_Named_Fields_Over_Positional_Variant_Payloads (rule id named-fields-over-positional-variant-payloads): a whole-file brace-depth scan (ported from rust_variant_shape.go's rustVariantScan) that tracks which enum body a line sits in, matches a tuple-variant-shaped line (name, then a single-line parenthesized payload with no nested unbalanced paren, then an optional trailing comma) at the enum's own depth, splits the payload into members at depth zero across <([/>)] pairs, and reports every variant whose member count is 2 or more, with a message naming the enum::variant and stating whether a member type repeats. Marker escape hatch '// tuple-variant: allow <reason>' (same-line trailing or immediately-above, non-empty reason required) using the same Has_Marker_Reason/Is_Skippable_Above shape concurrency_text.rs already established, duplicated per this crate's per-file convention. Rust-only, no repository-configurable dimension, so a leaf module rather than a capability. Own-implementation-file self-exemption, matching every other *_text.rs-shaped rule in this crate. Unit tests cover: a two-member tuple variant flagged, a single-member (newtype) variant exempt, a struct-form variant exempt (never matches the tuple-variant line shape), a K&R-brace enum, an Allman-brace enum (brace on the line after the header -- the corpus lesson itself, as its own named test), a nested generic payload split correctly at depth zero (HashMap<K, V>, u32 is a pair not a phantom triple), a repeated-type message vs a distinct-type message, and the marker exemption. checks.rs and lib.rs both declare/re-export Check_Named_Fields_Over_Positional_Variant_Payloads and NAMED_FIELDS_OVER_POSITIONAL_VARIANT_PAYLOADS (both re-export layers). The nomos-rules public surface snapshot is reblessed. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

items.title: no-wildcard-imports' use-super-star exemption cannot see across a split tests.rs file, and reports 49 false positives
items.why: Composing no-wildcard-imports into a real gate run (surveyed in an isolated worktree, not yet composed for real) reports 49 blocking findings, all the identical shape: 'use super::*;' as literally the first import line of a standalone tests.rs (or nested tests/*.rs) file. Check_No_Wildcard_Imports' own Rust_Wildcard_Findings_In exempts use-super-star only when the SAME file's own text also contains a textual '#[cfg(test)]' line before it (placement.rs's Is_Rust_Wildcard_Use_Line/exempt_test_idiom). That holds for an inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; ... } block, but this workspace's prevailing convention (confirmed: crates/agent/nomos-agent-executor-claude-code/src/lib.rs:241-242 is #[cfg(test)]\nmod tests; with the real content in a SEPARATE src/tests.rs starting 'use super::*;') puts the #[cfg(test)] gate in the PARENT file and the wildcard import in a CHILD file that never contains that literal text -- the rule's own textual, single-file marker cannot see across that boundary. Verified all 49 findings' paths against this crate's own super::Is_Test_Or_Example_Source (already the shared, established test/example-file-shape recognizer flakiness_text.rs and others already use): every one matches (a bare tests.rs, a *//tests.rs suffix, or nesting under a tests/ directory). This is a rule bug, not 49 real problems -- rewriting use super::* into explicit imports across 49 idiomatic test-module files would be pure churn with no clarity gained, the opposite of what the rule exists for.
items.done_when: Rust_Wildcard_Findings_In's exempt_test_idiom also treats use-super-star as exempt when super::Is_Test_Or_Example_Source(source) is true, independent of whether this same file's own text contains '#[cfg(test)]' -- the existing same-file #[cfg(test)]-positional path stays, for an inline test module inside an otherwise-production file, which Is_Test_Or_Example_Source does not recognize. A new test covers a standalone tests.rs-shaped SourceFile whose 'use super::*;' is its first line with no #[cfg(test)] anywhere in its own text, asserting no finding -- the exact shape all 49 real findings share. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green. run_context.rs composes no-wildcard-imports into Run (RULE_COUNT +1) now that it is safe to (0 findings against this tree), extending the doc comment's now-four-rule deliberately-absent list back down to three. cargo test -p nomos-check-orchestration is green. nomos gate run --root . --rule no-wildcard-imports reports 0 findings.

items.title: domain-values-are-distinct-types: a type alias that names a scalar but adds no type
items.why: code-standards' check-domain-type-alias (shared package rules/general/style/shared/domaintypealias, Rust front end language-kernels/programming/rust/rustlang/rust_type_alias.go, Go front end language-kernels/programming/go/golang/go_type_alias.go) flags a type alias whose right-hand side is a bare primitive scalar with nothing added: type EntityId = u64 in Rust, type EntityId = uint64 in Go. Verified against the real Go implementation directly: the judgment is Primitive and not Contract_Bound, where Primitive means the right-hand side is an exact bare identifier from a fixed per-language scalar list (never a generic or compound type, which is what aliases exist for), and Contract_Bound is Rust-only, true when the alias sits inside an impl or a trait body -- an associated type the contract declared, not a name the author chose. Go has no contract-bound case at all, so the Go side needs no nesting awareness. Four code-standards rule-doc ids exist (a cross-language canonical, domain-values-are-distinct-types, plus one companion doc per language); this port uses the cross-language canonical id, the same choice this crate already made for Check_Cross_Language_Correspondence. This crate's second whole-file brace-depth scan, generalizing the shape checks/enum_shape.rs already established (a pending-header, commit-on-brace state machine) from tracking one enum's own depth to tracking whether the current line sits inside any still-open impl or trait block, regardless of what other blocks open and close around it. This scan matters for real code in this exact style: nomos's own source consistently writes an opening brace on its own line after a header, the identical Allman-brace shape enum_shape.rs's own module doc already found necessary against a real corpus, so a naive same-line-brace assumption would make this rule silently useless here too. No repository-configurable dimension (the Go source's own comment states directly there is nothing here for a repository to calibrate), so a leaf module rather than a capability.
items.done_when: A new crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/domain_type_alias.rs implements Check_Domain_Values_Are_Distinct_Types (rule id domain-values-are-distinct-types): for Rust, a whole-file brace-depth scan tracks whether the current line sits inside any still-open impl or trait block (an impl or trait header committed once its opening brace arrives, cleared once depth drops back to or below its own opening depth), and every single-line type Name = Aliased; declaration outside that state whose Aliased is an exact bare identifier from Rust's own primitive-scalar-plus-String list is flagged; for Go, every single-line type Name = Aliased declaration (no depth tracking needed, since Go has no contract-bound case) whose Aliased is an exact bare identifier from Go's own predeclared-scalar-plus-byte-rune-string list is flagged. A generic alias, a compound alias, and an associated type inside a Rust impl or trait are all exempt. Own-implementation-file self-exemption, matching every other text-scanning rule in this crate. Unit tests cover: a flagged Rust primitive alias, an exempted Rust generic alias, an exempted Rust compound alias, a Rust associated type inside an impl exempted even with an Allman-style brace on its own line, a Rust associated type still judged once the enclosing impl has closed, a flagged Go primitive alias, and an exempted Go defined type (no equals sign). checks.rs and lib.rs both declare and re-export Check_Domain_Values_Are_Distinct_Types and DOMAIN_VALUES_ARE_DISTINCT_TYPES, both re-export layers. The nomos-rules public surface snapshot is reblessed. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

items.title: constants-are-the-exception-to-function-scope-use: a const buried inside a function
items.why: code-standards' check-constant-scope (shared package rules/general/architecture/shared/constantscope, Rust front end rust_constant_scope.go, Go front end go_constant_scope.go) flags a named constant declared inside a function body: a binding's scope is a claim about a lifetime and a constant has none, so declaring one inside the single function that reads it today claims the value belongs to that function, which is almost always false -- the next caller copies the literal instead of reaching into another function body for it. Module-scope constants and Rust associated constants (inside an impl, never inside any function) are exempt; the exemption falls out for free from only tracking function-body nesting, since nothing here tracks impl blocks at all. Verified against the real Go implementation directly (constant.go, rust_constant_scope.go, go_constant_scope.go): a single doc id, no companion per-language docs, no repository-configurable dimension at all (the shared package's own doc comment states it needs no calibration). This crate's third whole-file brace-depth scan, and the first needing a stack rather than a single slot, since Rust functions genuinely nest (a named fn declared inside another fn's body) while the two prior scans (enum_shape.rs, domain_type_alias.rs) each tracked a construct that does not. One deliberate divergence from the literal Go behavior, found while reading rust_constant_scope.go's own unconditional whole-tree walk: because it finds every function item anywhere in the tree and independently walks each one's own body for consts, a constant declared inside a doubly-nested function is actually reported once per enclosing function level in the real tool, which reads as an accidental side effect of a naive tree walk rather than a considered design the doc argues for anywhere. This port tracks a real stack (needed regardless, to know whether a given line sits inside any function at all) but attributes each finding to only the innermost enclosing function, a documented narrowing rather than a literal replication of what looks like a tool quirk. Go needs no stack at all: Go has no nested named function declarations, so a single optional slot, gated to only start looking for a new function header at depth zero, exactly matches parsed.Decls' own top-level-only restriction.
items.done_when: A new crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/constant_scope.rs implements Check_Constants_Are_The_Exception_To_Function_Scope_Use (rule id constants-are-the-exception-to-function-scope-use): for Rust, a whole-file brace-depth scan with a stack of open function scopes (a pending header committed to a pushed frame once its opening brace arrives, popped once depth drops back to or below its own opening depth) flags every single-line const NAME : Type = expr; declaration found while the stack is non-empty, attributed to the innermost open frame's function name, excluding a const fn header (which is a function modifier, not a value declaration, distinguished by requiring the token right after const to be an identifier immediately followed by a colon); for Go, the identical shape with a single optional slot instead of a stack (Go has no nested named function declarations), gated to only recognize a new func Name(...) header at brace depth zero, flags every const declaration found while that slot is open, including the parenthesized const ( ... ) block form. Own-implementation-file self-exemption, matching every other text-scanning rule in this crate. Unit tests cover: a flagged Rust const inside a function, an exempted module-scope const, an exempted Rust associated const inside an impl with no enclosing function, a const fn header correctly not treated as a value declaration, a doubly-nested Rust function reporting its constant only once (the documented narrowing from the real tool's own multi-report quirk), a flagged Go const inside a function, an exempted Go package-scope const, and a Go parenthesized const block inside a function. checks.rs and lib.rs both declare and re-export Check_Constants_Are_The_Exception_To_Function_Scope_Use and CONSTANTS_ARE_THE_EXCEPTION_TO_FUNCTION_SCOPE_USE, both re-export layers. The nomos-rules public surface snapshot is reblessed. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

items.title: A known validated range that contradicts the field type it decorates (Rust)
items.why: code-standards' check-scalar-range (shared package rules/general/style/shared/scalarrange, Rust front end rust_scalar_range.go) judges a struct field whose validator crate range attribute (a hash-bracket validate range clause naming min and or max) contradicts the type storing it: a signed field whose stated minimum is zero or above should be unsigned, and a field whose stated min and max both fit inside a narrower fixed-width type than the one declared should use that narrower type. Verified against the real Go implementation directly (scalar_kind.go's Is_Admitting_Negatives_Its_Bound_Forbids and Is_Wider_Than_Its_Bound_Needs, Narrowest_That_Holds and can_Hold_Range's exact tie-breaking and bit-width arithmetic, rust_scalar_range.go's attribute-clause reading). Two distinct code-standards rule-doc ids name the two distinct predicates (a-known-range-picks-its-type, nonnegative-storage-is-unsigned); code-standards' own finding model carries no per-doc rule id at all (a tool's Enforces line is the only place multiple ids are named, same architectural gap already crossed for the tuple-variant and domain-type-alias ports), so this port is two separate functions, one per predicate, each independently checking its own condition -- a field violating both gets two separate findings rather than one merged one, the same choice already made for the atomic-ordering family's three functions reading one shared value. No repository-configurable dimension: the bound is always the author's own already-written attribute, never a default a repository would state differently, so a leaf module. Scoped to Rust only for this increment: Go's companion front end reads a different struct-tag string syntax (validate colon min equals N comma max equals N) that needs its own separate parsing, not a trivial extension of the attribute-clause reader this item builds, and is left as a natural follow-up rather than folded in here. Simplified relative to the real tree-sitter implementation in one respect, found to be safe rather than merely convenient: the real front end pairs an attribute with the field beneath it by sibling position inside a parsed field_declaration_list, which this port approximates as a linear scan (accumulate a validate range attribute across consecutive attribute lines, consumed by the next non-attribute non-blank line) with no struct-body boundary tracking at all, because the validator attribute vocabulary itself is specific enough that nothing else in real Rust source plausibly carries it -- a function parameter list formatted one argument per line has the identical name-colon-type-comma shape a struct field does, but nobody writes this specific attribute above a parameter, so the narrower scoping the real tool's parser buys is not needed here.
items.done_when: A new crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/scalar_range.rs implements Check_Nonnegative_Storage_Is_Unsigned (rule id nonnegative-storage-is-unsigned: a signed declared type whose attribute states a minimum of zero or above) and Check_A_Known_Range_Picks_Its_Type (rule id a-known-range-picks-its-type: both minimum and maximum stated, and a narrower one of the eight fixed-width remedy types u8 i8 u16 i16 u32 i32 u64 i64 can hold that exact range, unsigned preferred at equal width, narrower than the field's own declared width among a wider vocabulary that also includes usize isize u128 i128 f32 f64). Both read the same linear attribute-then-field scan: a validate range clause is read out of a hash-bracket attribute line via balanced-paren clause-body matching and comma-separated minimum and maximum extraction, paired with the very next non-attribute non-blank line if that line is a name-colon-type field declaration whose type is in the declared vocabulary; a float-typed field, an unparsed or inverted range, or an attribute naming no validator range clause never produce a bound at all. Unit tests cover: a signed field with a non-negative minimum flagged, an unsigned field with the same bound accepted, a field wider than its stated range needs flagged with the correct narrower remedy chosen including the unsigned-at-equal-width tie-break, a field exactly matching its narrowest type accepted, a float field never bounded regardless of its attribute, an attribute naming no validator range clause ignored, an inverted range (minimum greater than maximum) ignored, and two attributes preceding one field where only the second is the range clause still pairing correctly. checks.rs and lib.rs both declare and re-export both functions and both rule-id constants, both re-export layers. The nomos-rules public surface snapshot is reblessed. cargo test -p nomos-rules is green.

items.title: OD-RULES-019: whether the five repo-policy providers owe standards.json one shared read, or independent parsing stays the accepted cost of one-capability-one-provider
items.why: A pasted external review names nomos-repo-standards/-limits/-scripting/-words/-goals as over-fragmentation: five provider crates each re-reading and re-parsing the same file. Verified directly against current HEAD (d9aeebcf): each of the five crates' src/reading.rs independently declares its own const STANDARDS_JSON, its own Discover_Workspace, its own filesystem.Read_To_String(root.join(STANDARDS_JSON)) followed by its own serde_json::from_str, and its own error type -- real, duplicated I/O and parsing, not a shared parse anywhere. OD-RULES-011 decided a rule's parameters are a repository-declared fact resolved through a capability contract, and established one-capability-one-provider-crate as the shape for the first family (naming); every later family (limits, scripting, words, goals) followed that same crate-per-capability precedent without OD-RULES-011 or any later record ever weighing whether the file-reading itself should be shared. This is a genuinely open question, not one already governed: OD-PACKAGE-006 and OD-HOST-004 cover hand-written registration and provider composition, not duplicated file I/O across otherwise-independent provider crates.
items.done_when: OD-RULES-019 exists, is registered, and decides whether the five repo-policy provider crates should read and parse standards.json through one shared reader (e.g. a nomos-repo-standards-json crate each depends on) while keeping their five capability contracts and five provider registrations distinct, or whether five independent reads is the accepted, bounded cost of keeping each capability provider crate self-sufficient -- checked against the real duplication measured (five copies of Discover_Workspace/Read_To_String/serde_json::from_str), not decided in the abstract. Does not itself build a shared reader; that is a later item's territory if the decision calls for one.

items.title: nomos-lang-rust-clippy's first-party filter drops every package under a relative root
items.why: nomos check's default --root is a bare relative dot (crates/host/nomos-cli/src/check/parsing.rs). First_Party_Relative_Root strip_prefix(root).ok()? treats a package_id it cannot relativize as a registry dependency and drops it, so under the CLI's own default every real workspace member is silently excluded and Require_Nonempty then refuses the whole capability -- verified live: nomos check --root . reports lint-diagnostics could not be materialized, nomos check --root $(pwd) (absolute) reports real diagnostics. nomos_lang_rust_cargo's own Manifest_Relative_Root (metadata_error.rs:254) already falls back to the absolute path instead of dropping the package on the identical mismatch; clippy_error.rs is the one asymmetric case.
items.done_when: First_Party_Relative_Root falls back to the absolute (unrelativized) path when it is not under root, mirroring Manifest_Relative_Root's unwrap_or, so a relative or mismatched root no longer causes Require_Nonempty to refuse every first-party package; a regression test in src/tests.rs proves a package_id that does not relativize against root still resolves rather than being read as a registry dependency.

items.title: checks/mirror states as current a twelve-universe count that is now three
items.why: The mirror module doc asserts in present tense that this workspace has twelve unmirrored universes, and leans on that number to argue the rule can stay green today. Three independent authorities all say three: tests/contract/tests/completeness_universes/table.rs declares UNMIRRORED_TOTAL = 3 and names FILLER_PATTERNS plus the two KNOWN_PROVIDERS; a live gate run over this workspace reports exactly those three completeness-mirror findings and no others; and an independent scan of every non-test slice constant in crates finds the same three. universe_kind.rs carries the same twelve inside a paired figure, though that one at least dates itself to 2026-08-09. OD-COMPLETENESS-002 exists because an earlier sentence in this same area said thirty-four and stopped matching anything measurable, so this is a recurrence of a defect this repository has already recorded and paid for once. Writing three in place of twelve would drift again the moment somebody mirrors a universe, so the durable fix is to route the claim to the authority that already declares and checks the number.
items.done_when: The mirror module doc no longer states a bare unmirrored-universe count as current fact and instead names the authority that declares and checks it; universe_kind.rs no longer lets its dated 2026-08-09 pair read as the present count; no live source comment in nomos-rules asserts that the workspace has twelve unmirrored universes; and cargo test -p nomos-rules passes.

items.title: Run re-ingests and re-materializes every source on every call, including subjects nothing touched
items.why: Reuse across calls is correct but buys no saved work. run_context.rs says so in as many words: reuse buys correctness of carrying state across calls, not yet a skipped recomputation for a subject nothing touched. The primitives to do better already exist one band down and are unused for this: nomos-analysis carries InvalidationReport, Broadening, Supersession and a DependencyPropagation walk over a dependents adjacency map. What is missing is the orchestration step that compares a subject content digest against what the store already holds at the current generation and declines to re-ingest or re-materialize when they agree. This is the first half of the efficiency invariant the design promises, and it is the single largest unbuilt piece of the deterministic kernel.
items.done_when: A second Run over an unchanged tree, reusing the same Workspace and MemoryFactStore, materializes no syntax fact it already holds, and a test asserts the count of newly materialized facts is zero for an unchanged subject set and nonzero for a changed one.

items.title: Only demanded invalidated facts are recomputed, and only affected rules are reassessed
items.why: The second half of the efficiency invariant: change set, then invalidate the affected dependency subgraph, then recompute only the demanded invalidated facts, then reassess only the rules those facts feed. Skipping unchanged subjects is necessary but not sufficient, because a changed subject today still drags every downstream capability materialization and every rule with it. nomos-analysis already owns the propagation walk and the invalidation report this needs; nothing consumes them to bound a run. Without this the analysis kernel stays linear in workspace size rather than in change size, which is the property the whole fact-identity and generation design was built to enable.
items.done_when: A Run over a workspace where one file changed recomputes only the facts reachable from that subject in the dependency graph and reassesses only the rules that read them, proven by a test that counts materializations and rule invocations against a one-file change in a many-file tree.

Declined.reason: Territory (nomos-analysis's invalidation.rs/propagation.rs) does not cover what done_when's rule-reassessment half actually needs: 'reassesses only the rules that read them' requires a skip mechanism in nomos-check-orchestration's Composed_Rules dispatch (run_context.rs), a file this item never reserved. The facts half is effectively already delivered by P40-INCREMENTAL-SKIP-UNCHANGED-SUBJECTS (8db1ae46): today's fact graph is entirely leaf/flat (every store.Materialize call passes dependencies: &[]), so 'facts reachable from a changed subject' already collapses to 'that subject's own fact' with nothing to propagate through. Re-authoring narrower, achievable scope with correct territory covering the real dispatch file.

items.title: Nothing constructs a non-empty suppression, baseline, adoption or coverage policy
items.why: The internal semantics of suppressions, baselines, adoption and calibration, and coverage are real and tested, but GateCommand documents repeatedly that nothing builds a non-empty one. A policy that only ever arrives empty is a policy nobody can use, and the tests that exercise it are exercising a shape no caller can reach. What is missing is the authoring and configuration surface: a declared, readable source a real run resolves these four policies from, so that suppressing a finding, adopting a baseline, or demanding a coverage floor is something a person can express rather than something only a unit test constructs.
items.done_when: A real gate run resolves all four policies from a declared configuration source rather than from defaults, a non-default coverage floor and at least one suppression and one baseline entry are exercised end to end, and GateCommand no longer documents that nothing constructs a non-empty policy.

Declined.reason: Re-added as -2 with a dependency on P41-GATE-SELECTION-COLLAPSE. The architectural review asks for no new gate policy increments until the gate stops selecting twice and compiles to one resolved run plan; this item as authored was claimable before that and would have added policy authoring onto the mechanism being replaced.

items.title: The gate has plan, run and explain but no compare
items.why: plan, run and explain are all real and CLI-wired. compare is named in the gate module as deliberately absent, and it is the verb that answers the question a gate is actually adopted to answer: what changed between two runs. Without it a baseline is a number nobody can diff and an adoption decision has no before and after. RunId already exists and is printed, which is the identity a comparison needs, so the missing piece is the verb rather than the addressing.
items.done_when: A compare verb takes two run identities and reports findings added, findings removed and findings whose disposition changed, is reachable from the gate orchestration seam the other three verbs use, and is covered by a test over two real runs that differ.

items.title: Declared phases, thresholds and approvals are named as unbuilt WF-001 gate semantics
items.why: The gate module names declared phases, thresholds and approvals among the parts of WF-001 it does not implement. A gate today is one undifferentiated pass over every selected rule: there is no way to say that one group of checks must pass before another is even attempted, no numeric threshold a run is judged against, and no approval that a human or an agent supplies to let a run proceed despite a finding. These are what turn a gate from a single verdict into a policy a team can actually adopt incrementally.
items.done_when: A gate run can declare ordered phases whose later phases do not run when an earlier one fails, judge a numeric threshold, and record an approval that changes a disposition, each covered by a test and each reachable from the gate orchestration seam.

Declined.reason: Re-added as -2 with a dependency on P41-GATE-SELECTION-COLLAPSE, for the reason given on P40-GATE-POLICY-AUTHORING: phases, thresholds and approvals are new gate policy semantics and should be built onto the collapsed selection rather than onto the transitional one.

items.title: COR-EXEC-001 says every correction operation declares its read/write sets, and none does
items.why: ReadWriteSet implements all seven resolution tiers and all four derived-provenance fields the requirement names, and its own doc admits it is free-standing, referencing nothing from CorrectionCandidate and not threaded into its constructor, so no existing call site changes because this exists. CorrectionCandidate, the type a correction operation actually is, carries only a ChangeSet, whose Touched answer sits at Artifact resolution, the weakest tier the requirement names. So the machinery is real and tested and the requirement is unmet: the committed assessment of COR-EXEC-001 records exactly this as its one gap. This is also the shape this repository blocks on elsewhere, a declaration nothing exercises.
items.done_when: A correction operation carries its read/write sets at the strongest resolution available to it rather than only a ChangeSet, the COR-EXEC-001 assessment no longer names CorrectionCandidate as a gap, and a test covers both a declared set and a derived one carrying provenance.

items.title: One correction family exists, so nothing has yet shown what generalizes
items.why: The phantom-mirror vertical is a real end to end proof that a finding can reach a deterministic type-state lifecycle and a filesystem commit, and it deliberately handles only the first recognized finding and only one candidate per run. That narrowness was the right call, but it means every generalization question is still unanswered by evidence: batching, ranking between competing candidates, and whether two families share a producer seam cannot be decided from a population of one. A second genuinely different family, chosen from a rule whose fix is not a text deletion on one line, is what makes the generalization decidable rather than speculative.
items.done_when: A second correction family over a different rule reaches Preview, Stage, Validate and Commit through the same lifecycle, the two families are produced through one shared entry point rather than two bespoke ones, and what the pair proves about batching and ranking is recorded rather than assumed.

Declined.reason: Territory named crates/host/nomos-cli/src/correct/second_family.rs, a location P40-CORRECTIONS-CANONICAL-SEAM (08949b65) has since emptied of composition logic: nomos-cli/src/correct.rs is now a thin renderer, and the phantom-mirror family's own fix-producer (phantom_mirror.rs) moved to crates/orchestration/nomos-correction-orchestration. Building a second family under nomos-cli's correct/ would either duplicate that seam or bypass it, directly contradicting this item's own done_when: 'the two families are produced through one shared entry point rather than two bespoke ones'. Re-authoring as P40-CORRECTIONS-SECOND-FAMILY-2 with territory in nomos-correction-orchestration, where the shared entry point (Run_Correction) now actually lives.

abandoned.reason: Releasing before decline: territory is stale post-P40-CORRECTIONS-CANONICAL-SEAM.

items.title: Correction product semantics live in nomos-cli, and nomos-api cannot reach them at all
items.why: Gate, work and spec all call canonical orchestration seams that both hosts share, which is what makes the claim that a host must not own product semantics true for those three. Correction is the exception and nothing marks it as one: the whole family lives in nomos-cli correct.rs and its correct/ directory, and nomos-api has no correct surface, so the second host cannot preview, stage, validate or commit a correction at all. Every later consumer inherits that hole: an agent-proposed validated fix, an API transport and an MCP surface each need a correction seam that is not a CLI module.
items.done_when: Correction planning and lifecycle are reachable through an orchestration seam both hosts call, nomos-cli correct is a thin renderer over it the way the gate verbs already are, nomos-api exposes the same verbs, and a new crate carries its band declaration, README row and contract-test harness entries.

items.title: A workflow step can only dispatch an agent or a model, never run a check
items.why: The workflow executor performs a real ordered sequence against real Claude Code and Ollama backends, which proves that workflow orchestration belongs in Core and can drive real work. Its module names check steps, correction steps and gate steps among the bodies it does not have. A check body is the first one to build because it is the cheapest and the most load bearing: it needs no external process, the check orchestration seam it would call is already the one both hosts use, and it is the step every composed Core workflow starts with. Until a body exists that is not an agent or a model dispatch, the claim that this tier composes Core operations rests on a population of one kind.
items.done_when: A workflow step whose body is a check runs through the executor against the canonical check orchestration seam, its outcome is carried in the same typed shape the agent and model bodies already use, and a test runs a two-step workflow whose first step is a check.

items.title: No workflow step can run a gate, so no workflow can end in a verdict
items.why: A gate body is what lets a workflow terminate in the judgment the whole system exists to produce, and it is the second half of the Check then Correction then Validate then Gate composition. items.title: The API cannot express gate scope or rule selection, so its gate run is not the gate
items.why: nomos-api reaches the canonical orchestration seams for the gate verbs, the work ledger verbs and the spec surface, which is what makes the second host real. Its own documentation records that the request surface does not expose gate scope or rule selection, and the committed requirement assessments name Handle_Gate_Run as a gap for exactly that reason. ScopeSelector and RuleSelector are real, and OD-GATE-017 drove selection down into check orchestration so an unselected rule can skip its materialization entirely. An API caller that cannot select is therefore not merely less expressive than the CLI, it is paying for every expensive provider on every call.
items.done_when: The API request surface carries scope and rule selection through to Run_Gate, an API caller can run a single rule over a subset of a tree, and a test proves selection reaches check orchestration rather than being applied after the fact.

Declined.reason: Territory reserved only crates/host/nomos-api/src/lib.rs. The real implementation, its existing call site, and the surface snapshot it changes sit in three other files this item did not reserve. Re-added as -2 with the full, grepped file set.

abandoned.reason: Territory reserved only crates/host/nomos-api/src/lib.rs, which merely re-exports. Handle_Gate_Run itself lives in crates/host/nomos-api/src/response/gate_run_response.rs, its only existing call site outside this crate's own unit tests is crates/host/nomos-api/tests/integration_seams.rs, and changing its signature from root: &Path to command: &GateCommand changes the textual line tests/contract/surface/nomos-api.txt records for it. None of those three were reserved, so the item could not be finished honestly. Re-adding as -2 with all four paths.

items.title: nomos-api is a serializable seam that listens on nothing
items.why: The application-service boundary is proven: typed serializable projections over gate, work and spec that both hosts share. What does not exist is anything that carries them off the machine. nomos-api documents that it does not listen on a socket and implements no transport, so the headless surface the design promises is today reachable only by a Rust caller linking the crate. Every remote consumer, and the editor surface OD-HOST-003 describes as a client of the canonical services, needs a transport before it can exist at all.
items.done_when: A transport serves the existing typed request and response surface over a real protocol, the seam crate itself gains no socket and no protocol dependency so the boundary stays where it is, and a test drives a real request over the transport rather than through a direct call.

Declined.reason: Superseded by P40-API-TRANSPORT-2, which is this item with the territory a new workspace member actually needs. The defect is unchanged and still open; what could not be executed was this item. Its territory reserved crates/host/nomos-api-transport/src/lib.rs alone, and a crate reachable from that file only does not compile, is not a workspace member, declares no band, and appears in neither of the two hand-maintained band tables a real gate run reads. OD-HOST-007 additionally requires the transport registry exclusion be structural rather than advisory, which is an assertion under tests/contract this territory could not reach either. Same subject, never published by either version.

abandoned.reason: Territory reserves only the new crate lib.rs, and a new workspace member cannot be built from that file alone. Re-authored as P40-API-TRANSPORT-2 with the eight further paths a new crate really costs, measured rather than guessed: the root Cargo.toml members list and workspace dependency table, Cargo.lock, the README band table, standards.json tier list, the two hand-maintained band copies in nomos-rules and tests/contract, the boundaries test directory that must gain OD-HOST-007 registry exclusion assertion, and the crate surface snapshot.

items.title: There is no MCP surface, which is now a clearer gap than the API itself
items.why: The intended headless projection is canonical application services beneath a CLI, an API transport and MCP. The first is proven and the API seam is substantially built, which leaves MCP as the sharpest remaining hole in that row: nomos-api states plainly that it does not speak the JSON-RPC framing MCP requires. An MCP surface is what lets an agent consume Nomos as a tool rather than by shelling out to a CLI and parsing rendered text, which is precisely the coupling OD-HOST-003 rejects for the editor surface. Sequenced after the transport so that framing and serving are not designed twice.
items.done_when: An MCP server exposes the canonical gate, work and spec operations as tools over JSON-RPC framing, an MCP client can run a gate and read typed findings without parsing rendered output, and no product semantics live in the MCP crate.

Declined.reason: Stranded by P40-API-TRANSPORT going declined, and stale on its own terms besides. Its done_when asks an MCP server to expose the canonical gate, work and spec operations as tools; OD-HOST-007, accepted after this item was written, decides the opposite for the first such surface: it projects the three Gate verbs and does not project the twenty-one repo-tooling verbs, because a transport that projected nomos-api wholesale would publish seven repo-tooling verbs for every product verb, two of which carry authority rather than information. Re-authored as P40-MCP-SURFACE-2 against that boundary and against the transport item that now precedes it.

items.title: An agent is handed a claim, not the typed task envelope AGT-001 requires
items.why: AGT-001 requires a typed envelope carrying goal, scope, applicable rules, prohibited changes, available tools and an expected output schema before agent work begins. Its committed assessment finds two of those real and the rest with no site at all: LedgerItem is the goal and territory is the scope, but Claim carries only who holds an item and when the lease lapses, nothing about what an agent may change or which tools it may use. Three separate requirement assessments name Claim as their gap. Nothing bundles any of it into one artifact, so an executor today is trusted rather than bounded, which is the wrong footing for a mutating agent.
items.done_when: One typed envelope carries goal, scope, applicable rules, prohibited changes, available tools and an output schema, an agent executor receives that envelope rather than a bare claim, and the AGT-001 assessment no longer names Claim as a gap.

Declined.reason: Authored on a false premise. Its why said no single typed envelope bundles goal, scope, prohibited changes, tools and output schema, quoting the committed AGT-001 assessment. TaskEnvelope has carried exactly those seven parts since 2026-08-24 in commit c00c5369, named P13-AGT-001-002-TASK-ENVELOPE-WORK-RESULT, and its own test says it closes AGT-001. The assessment is stale, not the tree. The real gap is that the executor accepts and ignores five of those fields, which is P42-AGENT-ENVELOPE-ENFORCEMENT, and the staleness itself is P42-REQUIREMENT-TRACE-STALENESS-RULE and P42-AGT-001-ASSESSMENT-CORRECTION.

items.title: No agent run reaches a validated correction, so agent output is never checked before it lands
items.why: A Claude Code executor and an Ollama backend both really run, and typed agent contracts exist, but nothing carries what an agent produced through WorkResult into a correction the system validates before committing. The game plan is explicit that an agent executor should not precede a solid mutation and validation contract; the executor was built first, so closing this is what restores that ordering rather than adding to the inversion. Until it closes, an agent either writes to the tree unchecked or produces output nobody applies, and both make the executor evidence rather than product.
items.done_when: An agent run produces a WorkResult that becomes a correction candidate, that candidate goes through Preview, Stage, Validate and Commit, a validation failure leaves the tree untouched, and a test covers both outcomes.

Declined.reason: Re-added as -2 with an added dependency on P42-AGENT-STRUCTURED-WORKRESULT. As authored it assumed an agent run already produces a canonical WorkResult; the Claude executor documents that it does not construct one from the model response at all, so the validated correction path had a missing prerequisite rather than a missing consumer.

items.title: The model routing vocabulary is declared and wired into nothing
items.why: The manifest vocabulary for model routing is rich and the README says outright that it is declared but not wired into a real consumer. The committed assessments agree and are specific: ModelExecutionProfile is the single named gap for four separate MODEL-ROUTE requirements, with Catalog and ResolvedModelExecution named for two more. An Ollama backend really runs, so a consumer exists to route to; what is missing is anything that chooses a backend by the declared profile rather than by a caller naming one directly. This is the same population-of-one trap the rest of the system has learned to avoid, one tier over.
items.done_when: A real model dispatch selects its backend by resolving a declared execution profile against the catalog rather than by a hard-coded choice, at least one routing constraint changes which backend is chosen, and the four MODEL-ROUTE assessments naming ModelExecutionProfile no longer do.

items.title: The fact store dies with the process, so incremental work cannot survive an invocation
items.why: OD-ANALYSIS-009 already frames the question of whether Run should read a persistent fact store instead of constructing one fresh per invocation, and leaves it open. Skipping unchanged subjects and recomputing only demanded facts both buy nothing across process boundaries while the only store is in memory: every CLI invocation starts cold, which is the case that actually matters to somebody running the gate. This is sequenced after demand-driven recomputation deliberately, because what is worth persisting and what a cache entry must carry to be safely reused are answered by that work rather than guessed ahead of it. It also brings a lifecycle with it, since a durable cache needs eviction, a version boundary and a way to be invalidated wholesale when the build variant changes.
items.done_when: The persistence question OD-ANALYSIS-009 leaves open is decided and recorded, and if the decision is to persist, a store survives process exit, is keyed so a stale entry cannot be served across a build-variant or contract-version change, and has a stated eviction and invalidation lifecycle.

Declined.reason: Stranded on P40-INCREMENTAL-DEMAND-DRIVEN-RECOMPUTE, which is Declined, as is its -2. Neither will ever finish, so this item could never become claimable. The ambition behind that dependency was not abandoned but decomposed: P40-INCREMENTAL-SKIP-UNCHANGED-SUBJECTS, P40-INCREMENTAL-SKIP-UNCHANGED-RULES and P40-INCREMENTAL-SKIP-COVERAGE-REGRESSION are all Done and deliver the currency machinery this item's own done_when needs. The dependency is therefore satisfied in substance and only the ledger edge is stale. work has no edit verb, so repointing means decline and re-add. Re-added as -2 with the dependency on P40-INCREMENTAL-SKIP-UNCHANGED-RULES, unchanged in territory, kind, done_when and predicate.

items.title: No provider uses a real compiler semantic API, so deep correctness evidence has no source
items.why: The language set is Rust and Go through syn, a scanner, Cargo, Clippy and cargo-deny. Every one of those reads syntax, manifests or another tool output; none consults a compiler for resolved semantics, so questions needing types, resolved paths, trait selection or borrow facts have no evidence source in this system today. The abstraction discipline here should be unchanged: do not build a CompilerProvider or LspProvider taxonomy first. Build one concrete provider backed by a real compiler API, let it expose ordinary capabilities like every other provider, and let it generate the evidence for whether any shared abstraction is warranted at all.
items.done_when: One provider produces facts from a real compiler semantic API rather than from a syntax tree or a tool report, it registers as an ordinary capability provider with a declared guarantee and determinism strategy, at least one rule judges what it produces, and no provider taxonomy is introduced for it.

items.title: main is at the August Phase-0 commit while dev carries the entire system
items.why: Every commit in this repository lands on dev and reaches main only by a merge, and no merge has happened since the Phase-0 state in August. The gate already runs on dev for exactly this reason, so the risk is not an unchecked branch; it is that main no longer means anything a reader could rely on, and the distance is now large enough that the first merge is itself a significant and untested event. This is repository management rather than product architecture, which is why it is a decision to be recorded rather than a refactor: what main is for, when dev reaches it, and whether anything other than a person is allowed to decide that.

items.title: A rule is a bare function, so the engine has to learn each one individually
items.why: A rule today is a function the composition root names, plus a RuleId, plus an entry in a hand-written mapping from rule to the capability materialization it needs. Nothing about a rule declares its own subjects, its required facts, or its applicability, so that knowledge lives centrally and grows once per rule. The package specification already says applicability is derived from canonical capability requirements rather than duplicated support information, which is the opposite of what the code does. A descriptor carrying id, subjects, required facts, applicability and judgment is the prerequisite for any planner: without it a planner would have nothing to plan from and would simply relocate the same hand-written table.
items.done_when: Every composed rule is reachable as a descriptor declaring its id, subjects, required facts and applicability alongside its judgment, the descriptors are the only place that knowledge is written, and a test proves the descriptor set and the composed rule set are the same set.

Declined.reason: Its done_when required the descriptors to become the only place rule requirements are written, which means deleting the hand-written mapping in nomos-check-orchestration run_context.rs. That file is not in this item territory and is explicitly P41-RUN-STOPS-NAMING-EVERY-RULE work, so the item could not be finished honestly inside what it reserved. Re-added as -2 with the migration left where it belongs and a mechanical parity test added against the already-exported Composed_Rules set.

abandoned.reason: Mis-scoped as authored; abandoning the claim so the item can be declined and re-added with a done_when its territory can actually satisfy.

items.title: Nothing computes a plan: selected scope and rules never become a resolved analysis DAG
items.why: The intended centre of this system is selected scope crossed with selected rules, resolved through applicability into rule requirements, unioned into required capabilities, reduced to a minimum shared analysis DAG where each required fact is materialized once, then judged. What exists instead is a sequence of conditionals that calls one materializer per selected rule family. The consequence is that capability work is deduplicated only by accident of ordering, the cost of a run cannot be known before running it, and every new capability adds another branch to the same function. A planner that turns descriptors and a selection into an explicit plan is the single change the rest of this critique depends on.
items.done_when: A planner produces an explicit plan from selected subjects and selected rules, naming resolved subjects, selected rules, capability requirements, provider resolutions and the analysis operations in dependency order; each required fact appears once; the plan is inspectable before execution; and the architectural decision is recorded.

Declined.reason: OD-RULES-009 has declined the generalized analysis planner across eight rounds of the same external review, most recently in its eighth amendment at this item's own occasion. The item's dependency edge is mechanically stale (P41-RULE-DECLARES-ITS-REQUIREMENTS-5 is Done), but repointing it to ready would put an artifact on the board that a governing record refuses. Three of the record's four triggers are unfired and the fourth is decided; the concrete cases that would revive this are named in OD-RULES-009's What Would Decide It.

items.title: Applicability is resolved during judgment, so the plan cannot know what it will not judge
items.why: Applicability is one of this system strongest ideas and it is currently answered late, per rule, while judging. That means the plan cannot say in advance which subjects a rule will decline, coverage is computed from what happened rather than from what was intended, and the same question is asked separately by execution and by coverage accounting. Once a plan exists, applicability belongs inside it: resolved once, driving which analysis operations are worth running at all, and read afterwards by coverage rather than recomputed.
items.done_when: Applicability is resolved as part of the plan rather than during judgment, the same resolution drives execution and coverage accounting with no second computation, and a test shows a subject a rule declines costs no capability materialization.

Declined.reason: OD-GATE-023. The only one of the five whose dependency on P41-RUN-PLANNER was load-bearing: it asks that applicability be resolved as part of the plan and read afterward by coverage, and its own territory is applicability_plan.rs. There is no version of it that does not need the plan OD-RULES-009 declines, so a decline is the honest terminal state rather than an indefinite stranding. It revives on that record's own named triggers.

items.title: Adding a rule edits central orchestration, which is the coupling the design exists to avoid
items.why: run_context.rs imports a concrete list of rule functions and rule ids, declares a rule count of 56, and its own documentation calls the rule to capability mapping a fixed, hand-written mapping. Every rule added since the first has increased what the composition root knows. This item is the migration that makes the planner real rather than parallel: all 56 rules move through descriptors, and the central function stops naming any of them. Until that happens the planner is a second mechanism beside the old one, which is exactly the transitional accretion this critique identifies elsewhere.
items.done_when: The composition root names no individual rule function, no individual materializer and no rule count; all 56 composed rules run through the planner; and a test proves a newly registered rule is executed without editing any central mapping.

Declined.reason: OD-GATE-023. The complaint is intact, run_context.rs still writes out seventy ComposedRule entries and Composed_Rules derives from that array rather than from DESCRIPTORS, but the question it raises now belongs to P74-RUN-ARRAY-DERIVATION-DISPOSITION: whether Run can follow the derivation composition::Registered already made, or whether needing each entry's capability slice makes that derivation the planner OD-RULES-009 declines. An item cannot both pose a question and be the work following from either answer. That decision authors the implementation item if the derivation turns out to be available.

items.title: Gate and Check each decide what runs, and the gate crate says so about itself
items.why: Gate filtered findings after Check ran everything, then Check gained real selection, and the gate keeps its own selector anyway. The gate crate states the result in its own words: the rule selector now layers a post-hoc per-caller finding filter over a Run that is already selective on its own. Two mechanisms answer one question, so a rule can be executed and then discarded, coverage can disagree with what ran, and a caller must know which of the two selections is authoritative. There should be one resolution of selected rules, compiled once, driving capability demand, execution, applicability, coverage and disposition alike.
items.done_when: A gate compiles its policy into a run plan plus a result policy, one resolved selected-rule set drives execution and evaluation, no finding is filtered out after being computed for a rule the gate did not select, and the transitional post-hoc filter is deleted rather than left beside the new path. The decision is recorded.

Declined.reason: OD-GATE-023. The defect this names, a rule executed and then discarded, stopped being true at OD-GATE-017: Judged_Sources passes command.rules.include to nomos_check_orchestration::Run, so a selected-out rule never materializes. What survives is Reduced_Findings re-applying the same include list to findings Run already restricted, which is redundant rather than two mechanisms disagreeing, and RuleSelector carries no exclude so the two cannot diverge. The done_when asks a gate to compile its policy into a run plan, which is the planner OD-RULES-009 declines.

items.title: gate plan describes the registry and does not vary with scope, rules or policy
items.why: The plan verb is the one place a person can ask what a gate would do before it does it, and today it answers the same way regardless of root, scope, selected rules, suppressions, baseline or adoption. That makes it registry introspection wearing the name of a plan. Once selection is resolved once and a run plan exists, the gate plan should be that resolved plan rendered: which subjects, which rules, which capabilities, which providers, and what the result policy would do to what comes back.
items.done_when: Two gate plan invocations differing only in scope, selected rules, or any result policy produce different plans; the plan is the same resolved object a run would execute rather than a separate description; and a test pins that correspondence.

Declined.reason: OD-GATE-023. Re-authored as P41-GATE-PLAN-IS-A-PLAN-2 without the planner dependency: the claim is verified still true at cff9df40, GatePlan holds only rules: Vec<RuleOffer> and its own doc says it does not vary by root, scope or rules, but making it vary needs only the ScopeSelector and RuleSelector that already exist and that Run_Gate already consults. The dependency was inherited from P41-GATE-SELECTION-COLLAPSE, not required by the work.

items.title: The filesystem port cannot list a directory, which is why every host walks the tree itself
items.why: The port offers Read_To_String, Replace_Atomically, Exists and Remove_File and nothing that enumerates a directory. Because of that omission every caller that needs to find files reaches past the port to std::fs directly, and check orchestration documents the walk staying outside for exactly this reason. That was defensible when one host walked; it is now the mechanical cause of duplicated walkers in nomos-cli and nomos-api and of the hardcoded extension lists in both. A port missing a capability that several real consumers need is a gap in the port, not a reason to keep bypassing it.
items.done_when: The filesystem port enumerates a directory, the standard implementation and the test double both provide it, at least one existing caller that reached for std::fs directly now goes through the port, and the decision is recorded.

Declined.reason:
Its own territory reserves only crates/platform/nomos-platform/src/file_system.rs and the
two OD-PLATFORM-002 record files, but its own done_when requires the standard
implementation to provide the new method too (crates/platform/nomos-platform-std/src/
std_file_system.rs, a sibling crate this item's territory never names) and at least one
existing caller to be migrated onto it. Discovered only after already adding the trait
method and starting the std implementation -- work has no edit verb, so the fix is to
re-author with the territory the done_when actually needs rather than widen a live claim,
which AGENTS.md and the nomos-task skill both name as the failure this repository has
already had twice. The trait addition itself (file_system.rs plus its own new test) is
sound and carries forward into the re-authored item's same territory; nothing about it is
reverted.

abandoned.reason: re-authoring with complete territory; see decline reason

items.title: Two hosts walk the tree themselves and each hardcodes the languages Nomos supports
items.why: nomos-api sources.rs calls itself a deliberate twin of the CLI walker, and both hardcode the same rs and go extensions and the same target and git exclusions, both reaching std::fs directly. That is two copies of the answer to which files Nomos analyses, in the layer that is supposed to be a thin adapter, and a third and fourth appear the moment MCP or a daemon exists. The specification puts file and project recognition in LanguagePackage and says every user-visible action gets a canonical application service rather than client-specific logic; discovery is currently the clearest violation of both. Recognition should come from registered packages and providers so that adding a language does not require editing every host.
items.done_when: One canonical discovery service resolves the source set, both hosts call it and neither names a file extension or an excluded directory, recognition comes from package and provider registration, and adding a language changes no host.

Declined.reason: Stranded on P41-PLATFORM-DIRECTORY-ENUMERATION, which was declined for an under-reserved territory; its successor -3 is Done and put Read_Directory on the FileSystem port with both the standard implementation and the test double providing it, which is exactly what this item needs to stop the hosts reaching std::fs directly. The dependency is satisfied in substance and only the ledger edge is stale. work has no edit verb, so repointing means decline and re-add. Re-added as -2 with three corrections measured directly rather than carried over. First, the walk is duplicated four times, not twice: nomos-api sources.rs, nomos-cli check/sources.rs, nomos-cli gate/sources.rs and nomos-lsp sources.rs each hardcode the same rs and go extensions, the same target and .git exclusions and their own nested-worktree detection. Second, nomos-lsp duplicates deliberately and says so in its own manifest, because nomos-cli check sources is pub(super), so the fourth copy is a documented consequence of the missing service rather than an oversight. Third, the territory now reserves all four call sites and the registration a new crate actually costs -- workspace members, the README zone table, the ZONES crate table and a surface snapshot -- none of which the original named, which is the same under-reservation that declined its own dependency.

items.title: A discovered file is a nomos-rules type, so discovery is owned by the layer that judges
items.why: SourceFile is declared in nomos-rules, and it is what the API and CLI walkers return and what the whole orchestration passes around. That inverts ownership: a discovered artifact exists before any rule does, and making the rules package its owner means the workspace, analysis and discovery layers all depend on the judging layer to describe their own input. It also means a future consumer that never judges anything still links the rules package to name a file. A canonical source or artifact representation belongs to workspace, model or analysis, with rules consuming it.
items.done_when: The canonical discovered-source type is owned by workspace, model or analysis rather than by the rules package, rules consume it rather than declaring it, and no crate depends on nomos-rules solely to name its input.

Declined.reason: Depended on P41-WORKSPACE-DISCOVERY-SERVICE, which this session declined and re-added as -2 to repoint its own stale dependency edge, so this item became stranded as a direct consequence rather than on its own merits. Re-added as -2 with the dependency on P41-WORKSPACE-DISCOVERY-SERVICE-2 and nothing else changed. Territory is deliberately left as the single declaration site: SourceFile is declared at nomos-rules lib.rs line 645 and named by more than twenty files across hosts, orchestration, languages and kernel today, but P41-WORKSPACE-DISCOVERY-SERVICE-2 removes four of those call sites and introduces a canonical service that may itself become the owner, so the consumer population this item has to migrate is not knowable until that item lands. Widening the reservation now would reserve a population about to change. Whoever claims this after the discovery service should re-measure and widen before starting, which is the step whose absence declined three items in this chain already.

items.title: A total order over 21 band numbers is stricter than the architecture it describes
items.why: Bands mechanically prevent upward dependencies, which is worth keeping. What is not worth keeping is that the answer to whether the gate may call check orchestration is derived from 40 being less than 41, and that the gate had to be renumbered to make a legitimate dependency legal. The system is a directed acyclic graph of semantic layers, not a ladder, and a total order forces an arbitrary claim of precedence between peers that have none. Named zones with explicitly allowed edges express the same constraint without inventing an ordering: host may depend on application service, application service on provider, provider on capability contract, and the reverse edges are forbidden by name rather than by arithmetic.
items.done_when: A record decides whether numeric bands are replaced by named zones with declared allowed edges, and if so names the zones, the permitted edges, and how two peers in one zone are treated. No code moves under this item.

items.title: The band table is maintained by hand in three places and a fourth checks it
items.why: Whatever the zone decision concludes, the mechanism that enforces it is currently a numeric table copied into the contract-test boundaries suite, into the dependency rule inside nomos-rules, and into the README, with a real gate run checking the third copy against the first two. Three hand-maintained copies of the architecture is the same unchecked-copy defect this repository has paid for elsewhere, and it is why a band change is remembered as touching three files rather than one. The migration should land the decided model once and derive the rest.

items.title: One semantic capability became one crate, which is not what a crate should buy
items.why: There are ten capability-contract crates and five repository-policy provider crates that between them read different portions of one standards.json, with a sixth crate existing only as the shared read boundary for those five. A Rust module already gives namespace and responsibility separation; a crate should buy independent versioning, an enforced isolation boundary, or independent installation. Where none of those three is true the crate is paying compilation and dependency-graph cost for a name a module would have given free. The judgement should be made explicitly and per crate rather than by continuing the current default.
items.done_when: A record states the admission test for a crate, applies it to the capability-contract and repository-policy families by name, and records which stay crates and which become modules. No crate moves under this item.

items.title: The tools that govern this repository sit in the same hierarchy as the product they govern
items.why: The README already names nomos-ledger, nomos-work-orchestration, nomos-spec-orchestration and nomos-surface-provenance as repository tooling rather than product, and draws the same line through the specification family. The risk is not that a tool ships by accident; it is architectural attention, and the evidence is visible: the specification database and the work ledger have absorbed a great deal of refinement while the central analysis planner is still a hand-written mapping. A physical boundary is what makes the distinction cost something to cross.
