items.title: Two cargo-deny discovery tests root at a literal whose deny.toml only exists on one machine
items.why: Test_Discover_Workspace_Should_Read_A_Violation_From_The_Json_Stream and Test_Discover_Workspace_Should_Refuse_An_Empty_Stderr_Stream in deny_error.rs both root at Path::new of F:/repos/nomos. Discover_Workspace requires root's own deny.toml to exist before cargo deny is ever launched, deliberately, so that cargo deny's upward search cannot silently pick up an ancestor's config. On this developer's machine F:/repos/nomos/deny.toml is a real file and both tests pass. On ubuntu-latest nothing is there and both fail with no deny.toml at F:/repos/nomos/deny.toml. This is the same class as P79 in the sibling clippy crate, with a different mechanism: P79's literal failed because it is only absolute on Windows, and these fail because the file it names exists on only one machine. The crate already has the platform-independent answer beside them: fact_context.rs derives Repository_Root from CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR by walking three parents, and the workspace root holds a real deny.toml. Fixing these two alone does not turn CI green, because the same crate's Test_Discover_Workspace_And_Materialize_Workspace_Should_Find_Every_Real_Policy_Violation fails on ubuntu for an unrelated and genuinely platform-dependent reason recorded in its own item.
items.done_when: Both tests root at a directory derived from the build rather than a hand-typed literal, so they depend on no machine's layout, and the crate's tests pass for a reason that holds on every platform rather than because the developer's checkout happens to be at F:/repos/nomos.

items.title: A cargo-deny provider test asserts this workspace has a duplicate dependency, which is false on Linux
items.why: Test_Discover_Workspace_And_Materialize_Workspace_Should_Find_Every_Real_Policy_Violation in fact_context.rs runs the real cargo deny against this repository and asserts at least one violation whose code is duplicate, justified by the comment that this workspace's own deny.toml sets multiple-versions to warn and this workspace has at least one duplicated dependency today. On ubuntu-latest cargo deny runs successfully and returns PolicyPayload with violations empty, so the assertion fails. The tool is present and the run is real; the dependency graph simply differs, because duplicated versions in this workspace arrive through platform-gated dependencies that do not resolve the same way on Linux. The test therefore asserts a property of one platform's resolution as though it were a property of the workspace. It is the last known failure standing between dev and a green run, and unlike P79 and P80 it cannot be fixed by making a path portable: it needs a decision about what the test should guarantee. Weakening it to assert only that the run parsed would remove the evidence that the provider finds real violations at all, which is the reason the test exists; asserting a violation only on platforms that have one makes the guarantee conditional in a way nothing else in this crate is.
items.done_when: A decision is recorded on what a real cargo deny run over this workspace is allowed to assert across platforms, and the test asserts exactly that: either a violation class that both platforms genuinely produce, or a guarantee that does not depend on which platform resolved the dependency graph, with the reasoning stated where the next reader meets it rather than in a commit message.

Declined.reason: Premise disproven by measurement, and the real defect is the opposite of what this item claimed. I wrote that the duplicates arrive through platform-gated dependencies that do not resolve the same way on Linux. Measured with cargo tree --duplicates --workspace: 35 duplicated packages under the Windows target and 33 under x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, including bitflags, hashbrown, itertools and rustc-hash, none of them platform-gated. Duplicates plainly exist on Linux, so zero violations is not a legitimate Linux answer and the assertion is not platform-dependent. cargo-deny is also installed on ubuntu CI, its own Test_The_Supply_Chain_Tool_Should_Be_Installed_At_A_Chosen_Version passing in the same run. So the test asserts a true, portable property and caught something real. Superseded by P81-DENY-PROVIDER-CANNOT-TELL-A-FAILED-RUN-FROM-A-CLEAN-ONE, which records what the code actually permits: Require_Ran accepts any Exited outcome regardless of exit code, deliberately, because cargo deny exits non-zero whenever a diagnostic reaches deny and does so locally with exit 4; Run_Cargo_Deny refuses only an empty stderr; and Violations_Of skips every line that is not parseable JSON of type diagnostic, which its own test enshrines. A fatal cargo deny failure that prints anything unreadable on stderr therefore yields Ok of an empty vector and becomes a clean policy fact. Weakening or fixturing the assertion, which is what this item pointed at, would have deleted the only guard that caught a false clean in a supply-chain provider.

items.title: The cargo-deny provider reports a clean policy fact when its own run failed unreadably
items.why: Discover_Workspace in deny_error.rs accepts a run it could not read as a run that found nothing. Three decisions combine: Require_Ran accepts any ExitOutcome Exited regardless of exit code, deliberately and documented, because cargo deny exits non-zero whenever a diagnostic reaches deny and does exactly that locally with exit 4; Run_Cargo_Deny refuses only a stderr that is entirely empty; and Violations_Of skips every line that is not parseable JSON carrying type diagnostic, a behaviour its own test Test_Violations_Of_Should_Skip_Non_Diagnostic_Lines_And_Malformed_Ones deliberately enshrines because real runs interleave noise. Each is defensible alone. Together they mean a cargo deny that fails fatally and prints anything unreadable on stderr produces Ok of an empty vector, which Materialize_Workspace then publishes as a clean dependency-policy fact. Nothing distinguishes checked and clean from failed and unread. This is not hypothetical. On ubuntu-latest the real whole-workspace run returned PolicyPayload with violations empty while cargo-deny was installed, its pinning test passing in the same run, and while the workspace demonstrably has duplicates under Linux resolution: cargo tree --duplicates reports 33 duplicated packages for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu against 35 for Windows, including bitflags, hashbrown, itertools and rustc-hash, none platform-gated. The exact stderr cargo deny produced on that machine is not known from here, because the provider captures it and it never reaches the CI log, so the specific trigger still needs a Linux reproduction. What is already established is that the provider cannot report the difference, and that fact_context.rs's own duplicate assertion is the only thing in the tree that noticed.
items.done_when: The provider distinguishes a cargo deny run whose output it could read from one it could not, and refuses rather than reporting an empty clean result for the second, with the discrimination resting on something cargo deny really emits rather than on an exit code the provider has a stated reason not to judge. The behaviour is covered by a test over a stderr stream that is non-empty and carries no readable diagnostic, which is the case no test covers today. fact_context.rs's whole-workspace duplicate assertion is kept, not weakened and not moved to a fixture, because it is the guard that caught this.

items.title: An integration test asserts that a cargo deny run which found no workspace still answers cleanly
items.why: Test_Discover_Workspace_Should_Run_A_Real_Process_Through_Nomos_Platform_Std_Launcher runs a real cargo deny in a scratch directory holding a deny.toml and no Cargo.toml, and asserts Discover_Workspace succeeds with an empty violation list, explaining in its own prose that this is a real invocation outside any cargo workspace that still answers, with no diagnostic lines to parse rather than a launcher failure. Measured directly with the real tool: that invocation exits 1 and writes one line, a JSON object of type log carrying level ERROR and the message that the directory doesn't contain a Cargo.toml file, and no summary line at all. It is a hard failure, not an answer. The test therefore encodes the false clean P81 exists to close as intended behaviour, which is why the guard breaks it. Two other tests in the same file fail for a duller reason: Diagnostics_Stderr folds cases into diagnostic lines only, so every fixture built through it now lacks the summary a finished run always writes. This file is not in P81's territory, so it is a separate claim rather than a widening.
items.done_when: Diagnostics_Stderr produces the summary line a finished run really writes alongside its diagnostics, so fixtures meaning a completed run are shaped like one; the real-process test asserts that a cargo deny run which could not resolve a workspace is refused rather than reported clean, naming what cargo deny really emitted; and the crate's integration seams pass for reasons that would survive the provider being wrong.

items.title: The gate installs cargo-deny after Test and Determinism, so the dependency-policy capability never runs in them
items.why: gate.yml installs cargo-deny in a step named Install cargo-deny at line 262, and that is the only place it is installed; there is no cache step and no earlier install. Test runs at line 98 and Determinism at line 145, both before it. Every test in those two steps that invokes the real cargo deny has therefore been running on a machine where the command does not exist. The ubuntu runner says so in its own words, now that P81 made the provider refuse instead of returning an empty list: cargo deny wrote no summary line, stderr error no such command deny, help find a package to install deny with cargo search cargo-deny. Until P81 the provider reported that as a clean dependency-policy fact, so nothing failed and the gap was invisible. The consequence is not a flaky test: the workspace's own bans, licenses and sources verdict has not been judged in the Test or Determinism steps at all, while reading as judged and clean. That is the false-coverage shape OD-COMPLETENESS-001 exists to refuse, sitting in the gate itself rather than in a rule. The fix is an ordering change and nothing else. items.title: The launcher timeout control asserts TimedOut using a program that is silent on Linux, so it is Stalled instead
items.why: Test_A_Program_That_Exceeds_Its_Timeout_Should_Still_Time_Out asserts ExitOutcome::TimedOut for a command given a one second timeout. Its fixture is not the same program on both hosts: on Windows it is ping -n 8 127.0.0.1, which prints a reply line roughly once a second, and on Linux it is sleep 7, which prints nothing at all. The launcher distinguishes a run that exceeded its whole timeout from one that went quiet, and a silent program reaches the idle bound first, so Linux returns Stalled with idle_elapsed of about 1.006 seconds where Windows returns TimedOut. It is deterministic rather than flaky: the Linux fixture can never satisfy the assertion. The test is the stated control that stops the timeout fix from being a removed timeout, so on Linux that control has never held. It was masked for as long as the ubuntu Test step died earlier, which P82's ordering fix has now moved past, and it is what that step fails on today.
items.done_when: The slow program the control uses produces output on both hosts, or the assertion admits both outcomes with a stated reason why either satisfies the control, so the timeout is genuinely exercised on Linux rather than the idle bound being exercised in its place. Run directly rather than under a shell, which the fixture's own comment requires and gives its reasons for.

items.title: The progressing-program control passes on Linux for a reason its own doc denies
items.why: Test_A_Progressing_Program_Should_Report_Timed_Out_Rather_Than_Stalled states its premise plainly: a short idle bound must not turn a program that is genuinely still working into a stall, and progress keeps resetting the idle clock, so this must still end at the wall bound. On Windows that is what happens, because A_Slow_Program there is ping, which prints a reply about once a second. On Linux A_Slow_Program is sleep, which produces nothing for its whole life, so no idle clock is ever reset and no progress is ever made. The test still passes there, but only because its idle bound of five seconds is longer than its wall bound of one, so the wall bound was always going to give out first whether the program spoke or not. The property the test is named for, that progress resets the idle clock, is therefore unexercised on Linux and has never been checked on any host but Windows. This is the same asymmetric fixture P83 corrected the other consumer of: A_Slow_Program is chatty on one host and silent on the other, and two tests read it as though it were one program. Closing it needs a Linux program that is both chatty and directly executable, since the fixture's own doc forbids a shell wrapper on the ground that it would put the sleeping process a generation away from the kill.
items.done_when: Either the slow-program fixture produces output on Linux as it does on Windows, so the progress premise is real on both hosts, or the test states that on Linux it rests on the bound ordering rather than on progress and something else exercises progress there. Whichever is chosen, no test claims a property that its fixture cannot produce on the host it runs on.

items.why: P42-AGENT-ENVELOPE-ENFORCEMENT was declined for an under-reserved territory and re-authored as a decision, P42-EXECUTOR-ENVELOPE-MECHANISM, whose own title ends in the words before code. That decision is Done and recorded as OD-EXECUTOR-007, which verified a real mechanism against the live CLI: restricted plus add-dir plus an explicit allowed-tools list confines file reach structurally, and a forbidden read and a forbidden write were both refused before the filesystem was touched. The implementation was never filed. TaskEnvelope fields are therefore still accepted and ignored, which is the contract running ahead of enforcement that OD-EXECUTOR-001 warned a first executor decides by default. Enforcing scope needs a real root threaded through Execute_Task, which has callers in nomos-cli agent dispatch.rs and nomos-workflow-orchestration run.rs, so it reaches beyond the executor crate.

items.title: One agent executor exists, so nothing has shown which of its choices are the contract
items.why: The Claude Code executor is properly bounded: fresh isolated working directory, strict tool configuration, a structural allow-list, one turn, a budget ceiling, timeout and stall handling, and structured parsing rather than trusting prose. A second executor over a richer session or harness runtime, of which Clay is the motivating example, would be an adapter rather than a new execution architecture. Its value is evidence: with one implementation nothing distinguishes what the canonical task contract requires from what one vendor happened to need. It is deliberately sequenced after the envelope constraints and the canonical result are enforced in code rather than merely decided, so the second executor is written against the contract as enforced rather than inheriting the first executor accepted-and-ignored fields. A harness executor gets no scheduler authority, no work-graph authority and no rule authority.
items.done_when: A second executor satisfies the same task contract with the same enforced constraints and produces the same canonical result type, what the two implementations disagree about is recorded, no scheduling, work-graph or rule authority moved into either, and the new crate is registered in the workspace members, the README zone table, the ZONES crate table and its own surface snapshot.

Declined.reason: Stranded by P42-EXECUTOR-ENVELOPE-IMPLEMENTATION-2's decline (its own depends_on target). OD-EXECUTOR-007 v2 measured that three of the four fields it decided (prohibited_changes, available_tools, applicable_rules via goal-text folding) survive the 2026-09-12 XVPE migration unaffected and remain buildable; only scope reverted to undecided. The precondition this item names -- a first real enforced mechanism to compare a second executor's choices against -- is therefore not gone. Re-authored as P42-SECOND-HARNESS-EXECUTOR-4, depending on P42-EXECUTOR-ENVELOPE-IMPLEMENTATION-3 (the re-authored successor to the declined -2) in place of it.

items.title: No agent run reaches a validated correction, so agent output is never checked before it lands
items.why: A Claude Code executor and an Ollama backend both really run, and typed agent contracts exist, but nothing carries what an agent produced into a correction the system validates before committing. The game plan is explicit that an agent executor should not precede a solid mutation and validation contract; the executor was built first, so closing this restores that ordering rather than adding to the inversion. Sequenced behind the canonical correction seam because a workflow or agent tier calling into a CLI module would invert the layering, and behind the canonical result implementation because the executor does not construct one yet, so this path would otherwise be built on a vendor-shaped response. nomos-agent-orchestration is the seam that should carry this: it already dispatches an executor and it is the application-service peer of the correction orchestration it needs, but it does not name that peer today, so an explicit zone edge is part of the work rather than an accident of it.
items.done_when: An agent run produces a canonical WorkResult that becomes a correction candidate, that candidate goes through Preview, Stage, Validate and Commit, a validation failure leaves the tree untouched, a test covers both outcomes, the new dependency is declared as an explicit allowed zone edge rather than left to the manifest alone, and the public surface snapshot is re-blessed.

items.title: OD-HOST-013: the three protocol surfaces are the engine's, and these crates keep only their verbs
items.why: OD-PLATFORM-003 settled that this workspace is an application over XVPE and moved the agent dispatch down on that basis, but left the same test unasked of everything else up here. Three crates were complete general protocol implementations with no XVPE consumer: nomos-api-transport held JSON-RPC 2.0, nomos-mcp held an MCP server, nomos-lsp held a language server. 'No consumer over there yet' is not a reason to keep a general capability here -- what decides is what the thing is. The line runs between carrying a message and knowing what it says, and all three had both halves welded together. Two duplications fell out of separating them: the line framing and the unrenderable-response constant were written twice, once per crate, and nomos-mcp reached its sibling by re-serializing every tools/call into a synthetic JSON-RPC line for that crate's own parser -- a round trip through a wire format neither side was reading off a wire.

items.title: OD-PLATFORM-003: the agent dispatch is the engine's, and AGT-006's no-dependency clause is retired for the XVPE crossing
items.why: This workspace had built a bounded agent dispatch -- a freshly created isolated working directory, an allow-list granting nothing real rather than a deny-list always one release behind, one non-interactive turn, a spend ceiling verified to abort before the expensive model call, a wall bound that kills, and an answer read from schema-validated structured_output rather than free text. XVPE's own reference miner had a three-line agent launch with no bound, no spend ceiling and inherited rather than captured output: a strictly worse version of something that already existed one repository away and that it could not reach. A general capability sitting up here was unreachable by everything down there. AGT-006's 'neither system shall depend on the other at runtime' was written on the premise of two peer systems; that is not the relationship these two have, and the clause is retired for this crossing only.
items.done_when: The dispatch, the capability boundary and the process port live in XVPE (xvpe-agent-execution, xvpe-agent-backend-claude-code, xvpe-agent-backend-ollama, xvpe-process, xvpe-process-backend-system); nomos-agent-executor-claude-code keeps the TaskEnvelope, the WorkResult and the schema, nomos-model-backend-ollama keeps its envelope adapter; nomos-platform-xvpe bridges any ProcessLauncher onto the engine's launcher surface rather than replacing the port's 33 implementors and 559 use-sites; Test_Only_The_Platform_Adapter_May_Name_The_Sibling_Workspace is deleted rather than widened into an allow-list that reads as a boundary while enforcing nothing; AGT-006 is assessed Diverges governed by OD-PLATFORM-003; the KWB crossing is untouched; and the crates the territory names are green.

items.title: Three providers inject a process launcher and then read the environment past it
items.why: nomos-lang-rust-clippy, -cargo and -deny each build a Command for the injected ProcessLauncher and then decide that Command name with a bare std::env::var("CARGO"), byte-identical in all three. clippy_error.rs does both in one file: Run_Cargo_Clippy takes a Launcher parameter, while Absolutized twenty lines above it reads std::env::current_dir() directly. A test that injects a fake launcher therefore still cannot say which cargo is run or what the root is resolved against, and nomos-platform has no port that could answer either. Measured 2026-09-12: 12 production std::env sites, 3 of them the identical CARGO lookup and 3 more current_dir; the 22 further sites an earlier count reported were inside out-of-line #[cfg(test)] modules.
items.done_when: nomos_platform::Environment declares Variable and Working_Directory, StdEnvironment implements it in nomos-platform-std with a Strategy triple like the other ports, and nomos-lang-rust-clippy reaches both through the port rather than past it, with a test that proves an injected environment decides the command name and the absolutized root.

Declined.reason: Superseded by P86-SURFACE-PROVENANCE-READS-THE-ENVIRONMENT-PAST-A-PORT. The finding stands and the port is unchanged; only the first caller was wrong. nomos-lang-rust-clippy cannot be the first caller because its provider is reached through nomos-check-orchestration public RunContext<Launcher, Fs>, and a third port parameter there means 45 construction sites across four crates. That migration is its own item.

abandoned.reason: The first caller this item named cannot be migrated inside any defensible territory. nomos-lang-rust-clippy::Materialize_Workspace is called by nomos-check-orchestration::Materialize_Lint, which reaches it through the public RunContext<Launcher, Fs> generic; giving that a third port parameter means editing 45 RunContext construction sites across nomos-api, nomos-cli, nomos-lsp and the orchestrator own tests, in crates three live board items are already working. Superseded by P86-SURFACE-PROVENANCE-READS-THE-ENVIRONMENT-PAST-A-PORT, which keeps the same finding and the same port and picks a first caller whose composition root is two hops away inside one binary crate. The port and its std implementation were written and compile; the clippy migration was reverted surgically rather than by git checkout, because those files also carry uncommitted step-2 work.

items.why: nomos-platform has ports for the clock, the filesystem, the lock and the process launcher, and none for the environment, so every read of it goes past the seam. items.title: A gate run narrowed by --include reports files as orphan modules because the lib.rs that declares them was not judged
items.why: Measured 2026-09-12 while finishing P86. `nomos gate run --include crates/platform/nomos-platform/src/environment.rs --include crates/platform/nomos-platform-std/src/std_environment.rs ...` reported three Blocking `no-orphan-modules` findings against those exact files, each saying "no declaration names it, so rustc never parses it and nothing in it compiles". All three were declared -- `mod environment;` and `mod std_environment;` were already in their crates lib.rs, the crates compiled, and their tests passed. Re-running the same gate with `--include crates/platform/nomos-platform/src` (the directory, so lib.rs is judged too) reported zero Blocking findings and exited 0. The rule decides reachability from the files in the judged set rather than from the crate module tree, so narrowing the set narrows what can declare a module. This is the worst direction for a narrowing flag to fail in: a caller reaches for --include to judge less, and gets a Blocking finding that a full run does not produce, about code that is correct. A reader who trusts it deletes or re-declares a module that was already fine.
items.done_when: A gate run narrowed to a single source file no longer reports that file as an orphan when its crate declares it, with a test that pins the case: the narrowed run and the whole-crate run agree on no-orphan-modules findings for a declared module. Whether the rule reads the module tree regardless of the judged set, or declines to judge reachability when the declaring file is excluded, is the implementation choice this item makes.

Declined.reason: Framed and territoried too narrowly, found while finishing P88. A second rule has the identical narrowing sensitivity: gate run --include crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/dependency/zones.rs reports two Blocking completeness-mirror findings (SAME_ZONE_EDGES and ZONES, each "resolves to no check, so this rule is declared enforced and never runs") alongside the orphan one, and all three clear when the include widens to the crate. completeness-mirror lives in checks/mirror.rs, not checks/orphan_modules.rs, so this items territory would have excluded its own fix, and its done_when named one rule when the shared cause is more likely the judged file set than either rule. Re-added as -2.

items.title: Whether the specification store seals its rusqlite connection, given that 107 production call sites hold it
items.why: SpecificationStore::Connection(&self) -> &Connection is public, and measured 2026-09-12 there are 107 production calls to it outside the owning crate: nomos-spec-bundle 52, nomos-spec-ingest 34, nomos-spec-project 18, nomos-spec-validate 3 (137 including tests). Those four crates therefore write SQL against SQLite own handle and each names rusqlite in its manifest. OD-SPEC-001 says the test that keeps the store trait honest is store-backend equivalence -- in-memory, SQLite and Postgres yielding the same store hash over the same corpus -- and that test is unreachable while callers hold the connection, because a query written against a rusqlite handle cannot be satisfied by any other backend. The record already declines to build Postgres and that is not in question here; what is in question is whether the seam it names can exist at all in the current shape. Note the escape is a method on the store, not a mention of the library, so a grep for rusqlite:: undercounts it badly -- that grep finds 65 sites where the real figure is 107.
items.done_when: A record stating whether the connection stays public, is sealed behind named operations, or is replaced by a narrower query seam -- and if it is to be sealed, what the first increment is and why 107 call sites is or is not worth paying. The measurement above is the input; the decision is which of those three the workspace takes, with the cost of each named rather than implied. Sealing is not assumed to be the answer: a store that grows one method per query is a different problem, and the record should say so if that is the conclusion.

Declined.reason: Its done_when requires a governing record and its territory reserves no record identifier -- only crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/src/store/specification_store.rs. A record is not governing until a file exists under docs/records/ and a registration exists under crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records/, and neither is reservable after the fact, so this item cannot be finished honestly as written. Re-authored as -2 reserving OD-SPEC-015 in both places, with the measurement and the question unchanged.

items.title: Three rust providers inject a process launcher and then decide the command name with a bare std::env::var
items.why: The finding P86 was written for, left unclosed by it on purpose. nomos-lang-rust-cargo/src/metadata_error.rs:150, nomos-lang-rust-clippy/src/clippy_error.rs:102 and nomos-lang-rust-deny/src/deny_error.rs:217 each carry the identical line `let cargo = std::env::var("CARGO").unwrap_or_else(|_| "cargo".to_owned());` inside a function that builds a nomos_platform::Command for an injected ProcessLauncher. clippy_error.rs also reads std::env::current_dir in Absolutized, twenty lines above Run_Cargo_Clippy which takes the launcher as a parameter. A fake launcher receives the command already built, so no test of these providers can say which cargo would run, nor what a relative root resolves against. nomos_platform::Environment now exists (P86) and nothing here uses it. P86 attempted this migration first and reverted it: nomos_lang_rust_clippy::Materialize_Workspace is reached from nomos-check-orchestration::Materialize_Lint through the public RunContext<Launcher, Fs>, so giving the providers an Environment parameter means a third generic on RunContext and its MaterializationEnvironment/RunEnvironment, and editing 45 RunContext construction sites across nomos-api, nomos-cli, nomos-lsp and the orchestrator own tests. That is why this is one large item rather than three small ones: the cascade is a single change and cannot be split by crate without leaving the tree uncompilable in between.

Consider whether the ports belong bundled -- P86 hit the parameter-count cap of 4 and bundled them as a Machine value rather than widening every signature, and RunContext is already that shape.

items.title: Two hosts each assemble the same std platform, and nothing exists for either to assemble it through
items.why: Measured 2026-09-12, inline and out-of-line #[cfg(test)] excluded: nomos-api names a concrete nomos-platform-std type at 34 production sites across 24 files and nomos-cli at 22 across 11. OD-HOST-001 permits a composition root to name a concrete provider and that is not in question; what is missing is anything for a root to name it *through*, so the same assembly is restated per host and per handler. The recurring shapes are the same in both: the pair `{ launcher: &StdProcessLauncher, filesystem: &StdFileSystem }` at 8 production sites, `AgentEnvironment { launcher: &StdProcessLauncher, .. }` at 4, `SystemClock.Now()` feeding Fresh_Run_Id at 4, and CorrectionEnvironment at 2. The sharpest one carries a correctness edge rather than mere repetition: nomos-api/src/work/ledger_at.rs:16 and nomos-cli/src/work.rs:46 each build FileLedger::At(directory.join("ledger.json"), StdFileSystem, SystemClock, FileLock::At(directory.join("ledger.lock"))) -- substantively identical, and each independently knows that a board is ledger.json beside ledger.lock. nomos-ledger owns that pairing and does not encode it (FileLedger::At takes a path, and cannot construct the lock because it is generic over CrossProcessLock), so a host that changed one of the two names would take a lock guarding nothing. Checked and NOT a defect: nomos-work-orchestration/src/run.rs:286 names the quartet inside its own #[cfg(test)] module, so OD-HOST-001s invariant that the orchestration crate names no concrete platform type still holds; and nomos-api/src/composition.rs is a deliberate twin of nomos-clis, because env! resolves against the calling crate.
items.done_when: A library crate under crates/composer assembles the std platform once -- at minimum the work-ledger composition that carries the ledger.json/ledger.lock pairing, and the launcher/filesystem pair -- re-exporting what a caller needs so a host names no nomos-platform-std type to use it. It is registered the way any crate is: workspace members, the README band row, a ZONES row and its SAME_ZONE_EDGES, and a public-surface snapshot. nomos-api work group is the first consumer and names no nomos-platform-std type afterwards, with its existing tests unchanged in what they assert. The other consumers -- nomos-cli, the gate and agent environments, nomos-lsp, nomos-surface-provenance -- are named as separate items and not migrated here, the same increment shape OD-PLATFORM-002 used. A Zone::Composer that would *forbid* a host naming a backend is deliberately not part of this: it would fail immediately against three hosts this item does not migrate, and belongs to whichever item migrates the last of them.

items.title: A gate run narrowed by --include reports Blocking findings about correct code, because the files that would answer them were not judged
items.why: Measured 2026-09-12 twice, in two different rules. First, while finishing P86: `nomos gate run --include crates/platform/nomos-platform/src/environment.rs --include crates/platform/nomos-platform-std/src/std_environment.rs` reported three Blocking no-orphan-modules findings against those files, each saying "no declaration names it, so rustc never parses it and nothing in it compiles". All three were declared -- `mod environment;` and `mod std_environment;` were already in their crates lib.rs, the crates compiled, their tests passed. Second, while finishing P88: `--include crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/dependency/zones.rs` reported two Blocking completeness-mirror findings (SAME_ZONE_EDGES and ZONES, each "resolves to no check, so this rule is declared enforced and never runs") plus one more orphan finding. In both cases every finding cleared and the run exited 0 once --include named the containing crate instead of the file. Two rules in two different files share this, so the cause is more likely the judged file set than either rule: a rule decides reachability or mirror-resolution from the files in that set, and narrowing the set narrows what is able to answer. This is the worst direction for a narrowing flag to fail in -- a caller reaches for --include to judge less and gets Blocking findings a full run does not produce, about code that is correct. A reader who trusts them deletes or re-declares something that was already fine.
items.done_when: A gate run narrowed to a single source file no longer reports that file as an orphan, and no longer reports its declarations as mirroring no check, when the containing crate supplies the answer -- with a test pinning both: a narrowed run and a whole-crate run agree on no-orphan-modules and on completeness-mirror findings for the same file. Whether the fix is that these rules read the crate regardless of the judged set, or that they decline to judge when the answering file is excluded, is this items choice. Territory names crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks because both rules live there; if the cause turns out to sit in how the judged file set is assembled rather than in the rules, this item needs re-territorying before it can be finished rather than widening quietly.

Declined.reason: Wrong kind and wrong territory, both established by measurement. It is filed as a Correction against crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks, and neither rule is where the cause is: nomos-gate-orchestration's Scoped_Sources narrows the source set before judging, so every rule that answers a cross-file question answers it against a truncated world. no-orphan-modules cannot be fixed in place either, because Test_Check_No_Orphan_Modules_Should_Report_Every_File_Of_A_Rootless_Source_Tree deliberately decides that a source tree with no crate root reports every file, and the rule cannot tell that real defect apart from a judged set that merely excludes the root. The item's second claim is also wrong: completeness-mirror does not clear at crate scope, it clears only at whole-workspace scope, because the tests that would resolve its named checks live in tests/contract, outside the crate. Re-filed as a Decision with the three candidate mechanisms and their costs.

abandoned.reason: Diagnosed. The cause is not in either rule and the territory cannot hold the fix, which this item's own done_when said would require re-territorying. Releasing rather than widening quietly.

items.title: The ledger owns the pairing of its document and its lock file, and does not encode it
items.why: Found while measuring P88 and deliberately left to its own item, because P88 reserved neither crate involved. nomos-api/src/work/ledger_at.rs:16 and nomos-cli/src/work.rs:46 each build the same composition from scratch, and each independently knows that a board is ledger.json beside ledger.lock in one directory. nomos-ledger owns that pairing -- it is the crate whose format it is -- but FileLedger::At takes a whole path and nothing else, so there is nowhere for the convention to live and every caller restates it. The hazard is not repetition: a caller that changed one of the two names would take a lock that guards nothing, and both files would still compile and both test suites would still pass, because no test in this workspace asserts that the lock a ledger takes is the lock for that ledger. The literals also appear in nomos-work-orchestration and nomos-ledger own test fixtures, which is where a rename would first look green. Note FileLedger cannot construct the lock itself: it is generic over CrossProcessLock and the concrete FileLock is nomos-platform-std, so the fix is to name the two files rather than to build them -- constants on the ledger that callers join against, not a constructor.
items.done_when: nomos-ledger names its own document and lock filenames once, and nomos-api and nomos-cli join against those names rather than restating the literals. A test asserts the pairing the composition depends on -- that the lock a FileLedger is given is derived from the same directory and stem as the document it loads -- so that renaming one and not the other fails rather than silently taking an unrelated lock.

Declined.reason: Territory short three paths, and its own done_when names one of them. It reserved file_ledger.rs and nomos-cli/src/work.rs, but done_when says nomos-api joins against the names too (crates/host/nomos-api/src/work/ledger_at.rs), the new names must be exported from nomos-ledger/src/lib.rs line 77's pub use store list, and naming them publicly changes that crate's surface, so tests/contract/surface/nomos-ledger.txt must be blessed in the same change. Re-added as -2 with all four, and with nomos-api and nomos-contract-tests added to the predicate.

items.title: Whether a zone rule should forbid a host naming a platform implementation, once no host does
items.why: P88 gave this workspace a composer and migrated one host; P88-THREE-HOSTS migrates the rest. Nothing then keeps them migrated. ZONES puts nomos-composer-std, nomos-platform and nomos-platform-std all in Zone::Substrate, and Permits lets Host reach Substrate, so a host naming nomos-platform-std directly is exactly as legal after this work as before it -- the composer is a convention with no rule behind it, which is this repositorys own written-but-never-wired shape one level up. A Zone::Composer, with Host permitted to reach it and not permitted to reach the platform implementations, is the mechanism that would hold it. It could not have been added by P88: it would have failed immediately against three unmigrated hosts, and a rule that must be suppressed on the day it lands is not a rule. OD-HOST-001 is the tension to resolve rather than ignore -- it states plainly that naming a concrete provider in a composition root was never the defect, so a rule forbidding it needs an argument that record does not already answer, and "so that a second backend set can be swapped in" is that argument only if a second set is real.
items.done_when: A record deciding whether the composer is enforced or left a convention, naming what it costs either way. If enforced: a Zone::Composer with its Permits row, nomos-composer-std moved into it, the README zone table and its contract test updated together, and a measurement showing no host violates it on the day it lands. If not enforced: the record says so and says what would change the answer, so that the next reader finds a decision rather than an absence.

Declined.reason: Territory too narrow, and the mechanism it proposed does not work. It reserved only zones.rs, but enforcing this needs README.md's zone table, a governing record, that record's registration, both derived projections, and an amendment to OD-RULES-020, whose own table declares the zone set. The mechanism is also wrong as written: a Zone::Composer holding nomos-composer-std forbids nothing, because nomos-platform-std would stay in Substrate and Permits already lets Host reach Substrate for nomos-model, nomos-workspace and five others. Enforcement requires moving the implementation out, not the composer in. Re-added as -2 with the measurement that decides it and the correct mechanism.

So a rule would land against zero real violations. Dropping the manifest edge is already a real guard -- injecting a use of nomos_platform_std into nomos-cli fails to compile, E0432 -- so the residual gap is exactly one line in a Cargo.toml, which is a smaller gap than P88 first claimed but is still the gap that four hosts independently fell into. The mechanism the declined item named does not close it: nomos-platform-std would stay in Substrate and Permits lets Host reach Substrate. Moving the implementation into its own zone does. nomos-platform-xvpe is not part of that move: XvpeLauncher is a generic bridge over an injected ProcessLauncher rather than a backend, the README already calls it one adapter and not a replacement for the port, and two Agent-zone crates depend on it in production, so moving it would fire on the day it landed.

items.title: Whether --include selects what a gate run judges or only what it reports, given that narrowing the file set changes what rules conclude
items.why: Measured 2026-09-12. nomos gate run --include <one file> reports Blocking findings about correct code that a full run does not: no-orphan-modules says the file is unreachable when its lib.rs declares it, and completeness-mirror says its tables resolve to no check when tests/contract resolves them. A caller reaches for --include to judge less and gets invented Blocking findings; a reader who trusts them deletes or re-declares something already fine. The cause is nomos-gate-orchestration's Scoped_Sources, which filters the walk before nomos_check_orchestration::Run sees it, so a rule answering a cross-file question answers it against a truncated world. no-orphan-modules' own module doc states the assumption that makes narrowing safe -- the two answers move together, a file the walk did not collect can neither back a declaration nor be reported as an orphan -- and --include is precisely what falsifies it: the file is collected, its root is not. The decisive asymmetry against OD-GATE-017's precedent is that selecting fewer rules cannot change a remaining rule's answer, and selecting fewer files can. Three mechanisms, each with a real cost. One: scope selects what is reported, judging stays whole -- fixes every rule at once and every future one, contradicts Test_A_Scoped_Out_Source_Should_Not_Be_Judged and OD-GATE-017's selection-is-real direction, and costs --include its role as a speed lever. Two: the run tells the rules its source set is partial, and a rule whose answer needs completeness declines instead of concluding -- preserves both, costs a parameter through RunContext, which P87-RUST-PROVIDERS measured at roughly 45 construction sites. Three: Scoped_Sources keeps each selected file's crate roots -- cheap and narrow, fixes no-orphan-modules only, leaves completeness-mirror lying, which is worse than leaving both, because a half-fixed instrument is harder to distrust.
items.done_when: A record deciding what --include means, answering OD-GATE-017's selection-is-real precedent rather than ignoring it, and naming which rules answer cross-file questions today. The mechanism it chooses, built. A test pinning the property in both directions: a narrowed run and a whole-workspace run agree on no-orphan-modules and completeness-mirror findings for the same file, and a genuinely rootless source tree is still reported, so the fix does not buy quiet by blinding the rule to the defect it exists for.

items.title: A dispatch's cost is exact integer money in the engine and becomes an f64 dollar figure before anything in this workspace reads it
items.why: Measured 2026-09-12, the whole float surface of this workspace's own data is five sites and this is four of them. xvpe holds a dispatch's cost as MicroDollars, exact integer money, and nomos-agent-executor-claude-code's own budget cap is one -- MAXIMUM_SPEND: MicroDollars::From_Micros(1_000_000), enforced by the engine against the same exact type. response.rs:39 then throws that exactness away on the first line that reads it: cost_usd: outcome.cost.Micros() as f64 / MICROS_IN_A_DOLLAR, carrying an as-cast-justified marker. From there the f64 is the only cost this workspace has: AgentExecutionOutcome.cost_usd, nomos-api's agent.rs parameter and its AgentExecutionOutcomeResponse, and nomos-cli's dispatch rendering. Nothing can compare a reported cost against MAXIMUM_SPEND exactly any more, and nomos-cli's own seam test already pays the price -- assert!((outcome.cost_usd - 0.01).abs() < f64::EPSILON), an epsilon dance around a value that was an integer two crates ago and only became inexact because this workspace made it so. The conversion is not wrong where a protocol demands it: AgentExecutionOutcomeResponse is Serialize and cost_usd is its published wire field. It is wrong as the internal representation, which is the numerical-abstraction convention this program is about.
items.done_when: AgentExecutionOutcome carries the engine's exact money rather than a float, and every internal consumer carries it unchanged. The f64 appears once, at each boundary that genuinely requires it: AgentExecutionOutcomeResponse's published cost_usd field, whose JSON shape does not change, and nomos-cli's rendering. The seam test's epsilon comparison is replaced by an exact assertion, which is the observable proof the exactness survived the trip. Prose in nomos-agent-orchestration, nomos-workflow-orchestration and nomos-model-backend-ollama that names cost_usd as the field carried between crates is corrected to name what is actually carried.

items.title: Confidence and the identity transition it grades have no consumer anywhere in this workspace
items.why: Found while measuring the float surface for this program's numerics axis, and it is a different defect from the one that axis went looking for. nomos-model's Confidence(f64) is the workspace's one bounded-ratio type and the obvious candidate for a numeric abstraction. Measured 2026-09-12: its only consumer is nomos-model's own Transition<Kind>.confidence, re-exported as IdentityTransition, and IdentityTransition has no consumer outside nomos-model at all -- the only Confidence::Of calls anywhere are the two in transition.rs's own test module. So the whole chain is complete, documented, tested and connected to nothing, which this repository's own record of its most common defect names exactly. Deciding whether Confidence should be a float, a rational, or a bounded integer is not answerable while nothing produces or reads one: every candidate representation is equally adequate for zero callers, and picking one now would be choosing a shape for a use nobody has stated. That is why this is filed as a validation rather than folded into the numerics work.

If it is, the item that will produce or read one is named, and the Confidence representation question is answered against that use rather than in the abstract. items.title: A gate step's install can be reordered after the steps that launch the tool, and only a comment says not to
items.why: P82 moved the cargo-deny install ahead of Test and Determinism and left a long comment at gate.yml:90-115 saying why it must stay there. A comment is what failed the first time. The step was ordered after Test for the entire life of this workflow, the provider reported a missing cargo deny as a clean bans/licenses/sources verdict, and nobody noticed until P81 made the provider refuse instead of returning an empty list -- so the defect was invisible for as long as it existed and the thing that finally surfaced it was unrelated. P82's own why states that the existing guard does not cover this: Test_The_Supply_Chain_Tool_Should_Be_Installed_At_A_Chosen_Version derives the step by name and asserts only that the install carries --locked and a digit-leading version, so moving the step does not disturb it. Nothing in tests/gate_step asserts step order at all -- the suite checks pinning, excuses, vacuity, and which step is the lint step and which the rules step, all order-free. The workflow is a file people reorder, and the cost of getting it wrong is a step that reports clean for a judgment it never made, which is the false-coverage shape OD-COMPLETENESS-001 exists to refuse.
items.done_when: A test in tests/gate_step asserts that the step installing a tool precedes every step whose command launches that tool, derived from gate.yml rather than from a list written in the test -- so a second tool added later is covered the day it lands rather than the day someone remembers. Proven by injection in both directions: the assertion fails against a workflow with the install moved back after Test, and passes against the real one. The comment at gate.yml:90-115 stays, and gains a sentence naming the test that now holds what it argues, so a reader reordering the file meets the guard and not only the reasoning.

Declined.reason: Its done_when describes a vacuous test. It asks that the install precede every step whose command launches the tool, derived from gate.yml -- but measured 2026-09-12, exactly one step textually runs cargo deny (Supply chain, line 333) and it already follows the install at line 116. That assertion passes today for the wrong reason and would have passed on the broken workflow too, because the step that actually needed the binary was Test, whose command is cargo test --workspace and never names the tool: the launch is indirect, through nomos-lang-rust-deny's provider. A test built to this done_when would be the vacuous gate this repository refuses. Re-added as -2 with the invariant that would have caught it.

items.title: A declared policy entry still resolves to a digest and still matches nothing in silence
items.why: OD-GATE-024 decided that a person names a sub-item finding by the subject_name the run already prints, that the comparison moves off the re-derived digest onto that name, and that an entry matching nothing is reported. It implements none of it, deliberately: the change reaches gate_policy_file.rs's entry resolution, the three Matches implementations in policy/suppression_disposition/suppression.rs, policy/baseline_debt.rs and policy/rule_calibration.rs, and the run's own reporting, none of which that record's territory held. Until then an author who writes a suppression for a name-addressed finding -- completeness-mirror, single-letter-names -- still gets no error, no warning and no effect, because Subject_Of_Path lowercases the name it digests and a name-addressed finding digests raw bytes, so an exactly-correct name cannot match.
items.done_when: A declared entry names a subject as the run prints it; Suppression, BaselineDebt and RuleCalibration match against Finding::subject_name rather than a digest the entry resolved to, with a test proving a case-bearing name-addressed finding is matched by an entry naming it and was not before; a file-addressed entry still works by its path; and a run names every declared entry that matched no finding, without failing for it.

Declined.reason: Under-reserved by its own author, found by grep before claiming rather than after. Moving the comparison onto Finding::subject_name changes a public field on Suppression and BaselineDebt, which reaches their constructions in policy/suppression_disposition/suppression_policy.rs and policy/baseline_debt/baseline_policy.rs, the crate's own tests.rs, two nomos-api response builders (response/suppression_response.rs, response/baseline_debt_response.rs) and two surface snapshots -- none of which the four reserved paths covered. Also split, because the two halves are independently landable and bundling them made an all-or-nothing change out of two that are not: matching by name is a type change across two crates, and reporting entries that matched nothing needs a field on GateRunResult, the reducer that fills it and the CLI that renders it. Re-authored as P76-POLICY-ENTRIES-MATCH-BY-SUBJECT-NAME with the measured territory; the reporting half is P76-A-POLICY-ENTRY-THAT-MATCHED-NOTHING-IS-REPORTED.

items.why: OD-GATE-024 decided that a person names a sub-item finding by the subject_name a run already prints, and that the comparison moves off a digest the entry re-derived onto that name. It implements none of it. Until it is implemented, Subject_Of_Path lowercases the name it digests while a name-addressed finding digests raw bytes, so an author who writes a suppression for completeness-mirror or single-letter-names and types the name exactly right still gets no error, no warning and no effect. Measured blast radius, because the field is public: the three Is_Applicable_To predicates in policy/baseline_debt.rs, policy/rule_calibration.rs and policy/suppression_disposition/suppression.rs, the entry resolution in policy/gate_policy_file.rs, the constructions in policy/suppression_disposition/suppression_policy.rs and policy/baseline_debt/baseline_policy.rs, this crate's own tests.rs, two nomos-api response builders that copy the field onto the wire, and two surface snapshots.
items.done_when: Suppression and BaselineDebt carry the authored subject name rather than a SubjectId, and their Is_Applicable_To compares it against Finding::subject_name; a declared entry names a subject as a run prints it, with the path spelling still working for a file-addressed entry; a test proves a case-bearing name-addressed finding is matched by an entry naming it, watched failing against the digest comparison before it is believed; nomos-api's two response builders carry the name; and both surface snapshots are blessed in the same change.

Declined.reason: Implemented, measured against the real suite, and reverted: the approach OD-GATE-024 decided is unsound as written, and the implementation attempt is what proved it. Finding::subject's own doc says it is derived from Finding::subject_name, never from a path. crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/formatting.rs writes the opposite -- subject: source.subject, the file's own path-derived digest, with subject_name formatted as path:line. So for the whole formatting family, which includes no-single-line-function-bodies and todo-format-is-todo-name-description-ticket, subject_name is not the preimage of subject and the two disagree. Moving the comparison onto subject_name therefore breaks the file-addressed case it was meant to preserve: the existing end-to-end test Test_A_Declared_Policy_File_Should_Tolerate_Findings_A_Command_Never_Mentioned declares paths b.rs and c.rs and stops matching, because those findings are named b.rs:1 and c.rs:1. There is no single field that matches both families today. The real defect is one layer down -- a documented invariant on Finding that a rule family does not hold -- and deciding the policy key before that is settled would ship the same silence under a different spelling. OD-GATE-024 is amended with this measurement rather than leaving the next session to walk the same path.

items.title: A rule family writes a subject_name that is not the preimage of the subject beside it, against that field's own documented contract
items.why: Finding::subject documents itself as Derived from Finding::subject_name, never from a path, and Finding::subject_name as the preimage of subject, so the two cannot disagree without the digest being computed from something else. crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/formatting.rs does compute it from something else: subject is source.subject, the file's own path-derived digest, while subject_name is the line-qualified path. Every rule in that family is affected, including no-single-line-function-bodies and todo-format-is-todo-name-description-ticket. The naming family holds the invariant properly -- subject is the digest of the qualified name that subject_name carries -- so the workspace has two rule families with contradictory readings of one contract. Measured while implementing P76-POLICY-ENTRIES-MATCH-BY-SUBJECT-NAME, which was declined because of it: no policy key can address both families while this holds, so the silent-suppression defect OD-GATE-024 was filed for cannot be closed above this layer. A reader of either field cannot tell which reading applies without opening the rule.
items.done_when: Every rule either writes a subject_name that is the preimage of the subject beside it, or the contract on Finding is changed to state what is actually true and why, with the reason a line-qualified name cannot be the preimage stated rather than left implied; the two families no longer read one contract two ways; and a test holds whichever answer is chosen, so the invariant stops being prose alone.

items.title: OD-GATE-024 decided a matching key that implementing it proved unsound
items.why: OD-GATE-024 decided that a declared policy entry names a subject by Finding::subject_name and that the comparison moves onto that name, resting on that field's own documented contract: it is the preimage of subject, so the two cannot disagree. The record's own premise is therefore false, its first three clauses cannot be implemented as written, and its fourth is independent and still stands. Leaving it accepted as written sends the next session down the path this one already walked and reverted.

items.title: OD-ANALYSIS-011 describes a mechanical guard that is false for 22 of the 63 sites it censused
items.why: OD-ANALYSIS-011 exists because Finding::subject and Finding::subject_name documented a derivation that does not hold, and OD-GATE-024 was written on that false premise and retracted. Its own What This Record Does Not Do section then sets the same trap one section later: it says a guard would be buildable -- assert that every finding's subject is either Subject_Of_Path of one of its locations or the digest of its subject_name. Measured 2026-09-12 against the real nomos_model::Subject_Of_Path, Normalize_Path and nomos_model::Content_Digest, that sentence is false. For a finding built by checks/error_text.rs Finding_At, subject is Subject_Of_Path(source.path) while subject_name and locations are both the path with a colon and a line number appended, so Normalize_Path keeps the suffix and neither arm holds: subject == Subject_Of_Path(location) is false, and subject == digest(subject_name) is false. 22 of the 63 Finding constructions under crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/ are exactly that shape -- 14 writing subject_name as the formatted path and line, 8 writing subject_name as a location variable of the same shape, all 22 paired with subject: source.subject, across 17 files including borrowed_container, closure_bounds, formatting, facade, enum_shape, error_text and the four text families. The derivation that does hold is Subject_Of_Path of the location's FILE PART, with the line suffix stripped -- a third permitted derivation the record never names, which is why a reader implementing the record's own sentence builds a guard that refuses a third of the rule set. Worse, the guard would not report that: nomos gate run over this whole tree fires only 8 of about 70 rules and not one finding carries a line-suffixed location, and tests/corpus fires the same 8, so no committed corpus exercises any of the 22 sites. A guard written to the record's sentence therefore passes vacuously today and refuses the tree the moment any of those 17 files' rules actually fires.
items.done_when: OD-ANALYSIS-011 is amended so the derivations it names are the ones that hold: subject is Subject_Of_Path of the file part of one of its locations, or the digest of the qualified name subject_name carries. The amendment states the measured census (22 of 63 sites, 17 files, the line-suffixed shape) and says plainly that the record's previous sentence described a guard that would refuse a third of the rule set, so the next reader does not build it. It also records that no committed corpus fires those 22 sites -- gate run over this tree fires 8 of about 70 rules and no finding carries a line-suffixed location -- so any future guard needs a corpus that provably exercises each derivation rather than a real run, which is the vacuity the record's own reasoning would otherwise walk into.

items.why: run_context.rs writes out seventy ComposedRule entries by hand while composition::Registered on the gate side already loops over nomos_rules::DESCRIPTORS. P41-RUN-STOPS-NAMING-EVERY-RULE was declined pending P74-RUN-ARRAY-DERIVATION-DISPOSITION, whose decline reason says in as many words that the decision authors the implementation item if the derivation turns out to be available. OD-RULES-027 decided it is: the census found sixty-two of seventy entries close over the same sources value, three of the four closure shapes collapse into one const-compatible fn pointer, and the residue is six entries reading a capability slice. items.title: The layering declaration a dependency rule judges against is compiled into nomos-rules and duplicated, stale, in standards.json
items.why: Check_Dependency_Direction judges every edge against ZONES and Permits in crates/rules/nomos-rules/src/checks/dependency/zones.rs, where ZONES is a Rust slice naming this workspace's own crates as string literals and Permits is a hand-written match. Two consequences, measured rather than argued. First, on any repository other than this one every member has no declared zone, so violations::Violations_In returns an empty vector at its own early exit and completeness::Violations_In emits one DEPENDENCY_COMPLETENESS finding per member: a foreign workspace gets a finding per crate saying it declared nothing, and silence on the layering question the rule exists to answer. Second, the declaration already exists a second time and has gone stale. standards.json declares a tiers array, authored by P26-DEPENDENCY-TIER-POLICY out of the README band table so code-standards' own dependency-direction check could read it. It names 50 paths under the band-N vocabulary OD-RULES-020 retired, and 16 of this workspace's 66 members have no entry at all: nomos-platform-xvpe, nomos-composer-std, nomos-lang-rust-compiler, nomos-repo-policy, the five nomos-cap policy contracts, nomos-connector-coderabbit, nomos-cap-requirement-trace, nomos-tool-package, nomos-workspace-discovery, nomos-correction-orchestration, nomos-agent-orchestration and nomos-lsp. Nothing in this workspace reads tiers, grepped: the only matches for the word are unrelated types in nomos-corrections and nomos-model-package. OD-RULES-011 already decided the shape a repository's own declared policy takes when a rule needs one -- it reaches the rule as a capability fact read from standards.json as data rather than compiled as a constant, and five families are built that way behind one provider in nomos-repo-policy. Whether the architecture declaration is a sixth family of that kind, or stays compiled because a zone table is this workspace's own architecture rather than a repository's policy, is undecided: no record argues either way, and the stale second copy is unowned while it is.
items.done_when: A new governing record under OD-RULES decides whether the declaration Check_Dependency_Direction and Check_Dependency_Completeness read becomes a capability fact read from the repository under check -- an OD-RULES-011 sixth family, naming the contract identifier and which crate would offer it -- or stays compiled into nomos-rules, and gives its reason against the two measurements above rather than by analogy to the five existing families. It disposes of standards.json's tiers array explicitly, as one of: the declaration a provider would read, a second authority to delete, or code-standards' own input this workspace does not own -- and where it is kept, names what makes the 16-member gap visible rather than leaving the reconciliation unowned. items.title: The record graph's typed vocabulary is one term in ninety-three percent of its edges, and that term is its own inverse
items.why: The seeded relation vocabulary is enforced by name -- OD-SPEC-011 made an unknown term a diagnosable refusal rather than a foreign-key failure -- and every type carries a declared domain, range and cardinality plus an inverse it is paired with, so Write_Relation completes each authored edge with its inverse on the way in. Censused across all 227 files in docs/records: 820 authored edges, of which 763 are relates-to at 93.0 percent, 51 affects, 5 affected_by and 1 supersedes. Every record declares at least one edge, so there is no orphan. relates-to is paired with itself, so those 763 carry no direction, and the one relation projection this repository commits shows what that costs: diagrams/relations.mmd draws 1612 arrows, 1500 of them labelled relates-to, each authored pair appearing once in each direction with the same label, against 55 affects, 55 affected_by and one supersedes pair. A reader or an agent opening it to learn how these decisions stand to one another is given 1500 arrows that say only that two records are connected. No record says what relates-to means or when a more specific term is owed. Of the seeded terms no record uses, the last four -- answers, answered_by, implements, implemented_by -- declare corpus node kinds (design-spec, feature-request, feature-result) as their domain and range, so no record could carry them; superseded_by is declared over record kinds and appears only as the derived inverse of the single supersedes edge. P10-EDGE-CONSTRAINTS was declined on the ground that the constraint mechanism was missing and the corpus would supply the real vocabulary. The mechanism has since shipped: domain_kinds_json, range_kinds_json and max_per_node are enforced in store/write/relations.rs. What is unmeasured now is not the mechanism but whether the authoring feeding it is honest.
items.done_when: A new governing record under OD-SPEC states the census above as measured -- 227 records, 820 authored edges, the four terms and their counts, and the 1612-arrow committed diagram -- and decides one of two things. Either relates-to is the honest term for a connection between two decisions, in which case the record names the cases where a specific term is owed instead and says why a 93 percent share is not a defect; or the record set owes a specific term where one applies, in which case it names the criterion by which a term is chosen and whether any mechanism will check it, without itself re-authoring 763 edges. Either way it states that the four corpus-scoped terms are unavailable to a record by their declared domain and range, so a reader stops reading their absence as neglect. It states what it does not do: no relation is re-authored, no seed table changes, no projection changes, and diagrams/relations.mmd is not regenerated for content reasons by this item. Registered at crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records/OD-SPEC-015.record so it is governing rather than merely written, and cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nomos-spec-store -p nomos-contract-tests passes.

items.title: A record's declared status is stored and cannot be selected, so ten open governing questions project as settled decisions
items.why: Migration 5 created record_front_matter for the three fields the graph could not hold -- status, version and tags -- and authoring/write.rs fills it for every record the store seeds. Nothing reads status back out. nomos_spec_project::Filter carries eleven fields (kind, authority, representation, suite, document, revision, relation_type, disposition, row_kind, identifier_prefix, node_id) and none is status; the nodes selection in select/sections.rs reads node_id, kind, authority, representation, title and suite_id from nodes with no join to record_front_matter. So no profile can select on a record's lifecycle status and no projection can show it. Measured over docs/records: 227 records carry three values -- accepted 195, closed 22, open 10 -- and the ten open ones are this repository's own unanswered governing questions, among them OD-RULES-007 on a rule-program intermediate representation, OD-CAPABILITY-007 on a declared decline-with-reason, OD-SPEC-001 on the storage backend and OD-LEDGER-001 on territory being declared and not enforced. In spec/domain-specification.md, the one markdown projection this repository commits, those ten render beside the 195 accepted ones with nothing distinguishing them; the only occurrences of the word status in that file are the literal Status headings inside record bodies. The projection an agent is routed to therefore presents an open question as a settled decision, and the field that would have said otherwise is one join away.
items.done_when: nomos_spec_project::Filter gains a status field. select.rs admits it for the content kinds that can answer it and refuses it through the existing ProjectError::UnsupportedFilter for the kinds that cannot, the same way an unsupported filter is already refused. The nodes selection joins record_front_matter so a status filter narrows on the value a record declared, and a node with no front-matter row (a referenced placeholder) is excluded rather than reported with an invented status. The shipped html-site profile gains a section selecting nodes whose declared status is open, so the field has a real consumer rather than a test-only one: html-site renders on a records-only store per OD-PROJECT-002 and is not a committed output per OD-PROJECT-003, so no freshness obligation and no committed projection moves. tests/projections/selection.rs gains a case proving a status filter over a real seeded store selects the open records and excludes the accepted ones, and a case proving the unsupported-kind refusal names the filter. tests/contract/surface/nomos-spec-project.txt is updated for the one new public field. cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nomos-spec-project -p nomos-contract-tests passes.

items.title: The HTML projection resolves no identifier, so it gives a reader strictly less than the markdown rendered from the same store
items.why: Render_Html in crates/spec/nomos-spec-project/src/render.rs writes a head, one section element per profile section, and one article per item; Write_Article writes the item identity as an h3, its stated fields as a definition list, and its body in a pre. There is no anchor element anywhere in the renderer -- grepped: no a element, no href, no nav, no per-item id attribute -- so every identifier a projection carries is escaped text a reader cannot follow, including both endpoints of every row in the Relations section that traceability-matrix and subject-report select. Slug_Of_Text already exists and is spent only on the section id, so a section is addressable and an item is not. Two shipped profiles declare format html, html-site and subject-report, and both render this way. The markdown renderer beside it produces output GitHub resolves for the same content, so the html format currently gives a reader less than the format it was presumably added to improve on: no cross-reference, no backlink, no way to reach a record from the edge naming it. What an html projection must add over markdown is undecided -- OD-PROJECT-002 decided which projections are required and OD-PROJECT-003 what committing one costs, and neither answers this -- but the gap does not need a decision first: an identifier resolving to the item it names inside the same projection is what the format is for, and nothing about it is contested.
items.done_when: Render_Html gives every item a stable id derived from its identity through the existing Slug_Of_Text, and renders an identifier naming another item in the same projection as a link to that item's id rather than as escaped text -- at minimum both endpoints of a Relations row. An identity no item in the projection carries stays plain text rather than becoming a dead link. Escaping is unchanged: an identity carrying an html-significant character is still escaped before it reaches an attribute or a body, and the escaping used for an attribute value is correct for that position rather than reusing the body escape unexamined. tests/projections/renderers.rs gains three cases: a relation endpoint present in the projection renders as a link to that item's id, an endpoint absent from it renders as text, and an identity carrying a character that would break an attribute is escaped there. Determinism does not move: the existing determinism contract still passes, so two renders of one store stay byte-identical. cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nomos-spec-project -p nomos-contract-tests passes.

items.title: Ledger validation checks that a dependency resolves and not that the graph the dependencies form is acyclic
items.why: Validate_Document runs five per-item checks and two document-wide ones: duplicate identifiers, dependencies naming an item the ledger does not hold, state coherence, predicate, territory, patterns, and overlapping claims. None looks at the shape of the dependency graph. Two items naming each other in depends_on, or any longer ring, is a valid document by this function and therefore loads -- Load refuses an invalid document and every verb loads first, so nothing downstream examines it again. A cycle then produces silence rather than an error. Every item in the ring lists as waiting, the label for a dependency that has not finished, and stays that way forever because no member can finish before another member that cannot finish either. The next line OD-LEDGER-023 computes from the whole board never names any of them. And stranded, the one label that says a dependency will never finish, is reserved by OD-LEDGER-020 for a declined dependency and does not fire here. Measured on the live board: 1148 items, no cycle, no self-dependency, no dangling dependency -- so this is a guard against a defect that has not happened rather than a repair, and a provably clean board is the cheapest moment to add one. The class is one this ledger already writes records about: a coordination document whose validator checks that a reference resolves and not that the structure those references form is usable. OD-LEDGER-038, on an item ended honestly leaving others silently unreachable, is the same failure mode reached by a different route.
items.done_when: Validate_Document reports a violation for each dependency cycle in the document, naming the items in the ring in a stable order rather than emitting one violation per member, and the seven existing checks are unchanged in what they report. The violation text follows the existing convention in this file: it names the subject so a caller can act on it. A test in validation.rs proves it on four shapes -- a two-item mutual pair, a longer ring, a self-dependency named either as a cycle of one or as already covered by an existing check depending on which the implementation finds true, and an acyclic diamond that must not be reported, which is the negative control and must be confirmed red before the check is written. The live board still validates: nomos work validate exits 0 against work/ledger.json. cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nomos-ledger -p nomos-contract-tests passes.

items.title: The implementation context pack selects every decision and every statement, and selection cannot follow a relation at all
items.why: implementation-context-pack is the one profile whose declared format is contextpack and whose output is context/implementation.json -- the shape meant to be an agent's focused context. Its three sections are every node of kind decision, every normative statement with no filter at all, and every prose block. Nothing scopes it to a task, a subject or a question. Selection cannot do better: Filter is a flat conjunction of equality, prefix and either-column clauses over one table, and no code path in select follows an edge. subject-dossier, the nearest thing to a scoped projection, selects the subject's own node, its own statements and its own relation rows, and those rows are listed rather than resolved, so a neighbour's content is never retrieved and a second hop does not exist. So the projection meant to be focused is the least focused one shipped, and an agent needing the record that governs the thing it is about to change must either read the whole decision set or already know the identifier -- which is the condition a context pack exists to remove. What a bounded traversal would have to settle is not obvious, which is why this is a decision before it is code: which relation terms are worth following at all given that 93 percent of this record graph's edges are relates-to and relates-to is its own inverse, whether the stop condition is a hop bound or a node budget, whether a record's declared status participates in what is followed, in what order reached content is emitted so two renders of one store stay byte-identical under the existing determinism contract, and whether reached content is inlined or cited by identity and section anchor.
items.done_when: A new governing record under OD-PROJECT decides whether projection selection gains bounded relation traversal. If it does, the record fixes all five questions above: which terms are followed, the stop condition, whether declared status participates, the emission order that keeps rendering deterministic, and inlined content versus citation by identity and anchor. If it declines, it says what a caller does instead and measures that answer against what the shipped profiles can express today rather than against the idea of a context pack. Either way it states the three facts above as measured: the three unscoped sections of implementation-context-pack, the flat shape of Filter, and that subject-dossier lists relation rows without resolving them. It states what it does not do: no profile changes, no selection code, no new filter field, no renderer change. Registered at crates/spec/nomos-spec-store/records/OD-PROJECT-005.record so it is governing rather than merely written, and cargo test --no-fail-fast -p nomos-spec-store -p nomos-contract-tests passes.
